notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1243.tmp1243.opp-lat: Letter I: 'iudicare' read as 'indicare' (make known). 'diacoposin' is obscure (apparently a Greek term, perhaps a military or administrative arrangement); kept untranslated. Stray letters after 'Presbyterum', 'Autisiodorensem' and 'Epistola' are footnote marks. Letter II: the addressee is given as both Aunacharius and Aunarius. Letter III: 'reliquit [redegit]' and 'clamanter [clamantes]' follow the editor's bracketed corrections; 'fides na' read as 'fides tua'.

Line 8: the clause after 'eligite' is compressed; 'ad placita satisfactionis reddere rationem' is rendered loosely. 'Audite potestatem et commonentem' (line 10) seems corrupt, perhaps for 'protestantem'. Line 12: 'nec eos aliter ... dirigere pertulistis, ut ... se paterentur accipere' is awkward and probably corrupt; the sense seems to be that the envoys were not allowed to accept satisfaction. 'expressisset' lacks a clear subject (the letter?). The Ephesians citation 'Ephes. v' is properly Eph. 4.

In 14, 'polypticis' is taken as 'registers' (polyptycha). In 18, 'plebis sansfactionibus' is read as 'plenis satisfactionibus' (Cyprian's text), 'with full satisfactions'. In 16, Cyprian's treatise is De unitate ecclesiae; 'mutavit' is read as 'titulavit/notavit' (entitled). The Augustine passage is a paraphrase, not a verbatim quotation.

In section I several readings are corrupt: 'palmites .utendo' is taken as 'palmites putando' (pruning); 'indisrete inventionis increpamur, qua' is taken as a reproach (invectione) by which the Lord speaks; the Gilead sentence ('nisi in Scripturae sacrae altitudinem innumera sententiarum densitas dicit') is garbled and rendered by sense; 'susceptionum' is read as 'suspicionum' (suspicions). The quotation 'Is there no resin in Gilead...' is from Jer. 8:22, not Ezek. 34 as the edition's reference gives; the preceding quotation is from Ezek. 34. The Pauline citation is 1 Cor. 12:26 (edition: XI). In section II the closing phrase 'quasi quaedam se mundo, nobis infudit' is defective; rendered following the editor's conjecture 'lux mundo'.

Line 24: in the first Leo quotation 'quæ tanta per Spiritum sanctum filii auctoritas' is corrupt; translated as if 'fulciuntur auctoritate' ('upheld by such authority'). 'decli- nati' read as 'declinatis'; 'viVere [respicere]' read as 'respicere'; 'Me!' read as 'fidei'. The sentence 'Qui ergo unit cum Chalcedonensi synodo...' is corrupt (perhaps 'uni... convenit' or 'renuit'); translated by the evident sense. The parenthesis '(solam nihilominus exciperet) (a)' is obscure and its sense uncertain. 'private' read as 'privatim', 'moto' as 'mota'. Line 25: 'icta' read as 'iota'; the sentence beginning 'Neque enim iota unum' is the Encyclia's actual wording, introduced here with 'but thus' supplied in sense.

Line 27: 'non lusi sacrilegus' is obscure; read as 'non lusor sed sacrilegus' (reopener found to be not a trifler but sacrilegious) — uncertain. 'Pie... utendum' read with the edition's marginal 'vivendum' sense; 'aliquam' as 'ad aliquam'; 'imprimitur'/'attenditur' as 'exprimitur'/'ostenditur' per the edition's suggestions. Line 29: the bracket '[Forsan mutat' is unclosed and the text garbled; translated as 'consilium non mutat, saepe sententiam mutat'. Biblical reference 'Galat. I' should be Gal. 2; '1 Reg. xv' = 1 Samuel 15.

Line 30: the sentence 'Et si Jesum ... damnavit' is garbled in the edition; it is rendered as an implied question whether Theodore, in effect, condemned Christ. Line 31: the quoted Theodore passage is corrupt in places ('nisi forte ... non jubes', 'Inerat forsitan', and the final conditional); translated as closely as the text allows. Bracketed alternative readings printed by the edition (e.g. [virtutem], [præformationem ... sperationis], Al.) are translated in brackets. In line 40 'tomus' of Proclus is rendered 'tome' (lower case), as it is Proclus' Tome to the Armenians, not the Tome of Leo.

XII: the name Rabbula is supplied in brackets by the edition. XVI: the edition reads 'Theodoreti' with the correction 'Ibae' in brackets; the letter in question is that of Ibas, though the text twice names Theodoret. XVI: 'Deus tacetur' is obscure; it seems to mean that the Theodore–Nestorius teaching keeps silent about [his being] God. XVII: 'Vestrae fidei fundamentum tenemus' is odd in context ('we hold the foundation of your faith'); 'nostrae' may be meant.

Line 47: the emperor's words contain a garbled doublet ('firmari potius per synodum formari'); translated as 'confirmed... through the synod'. 'Quae reverendissimi episcopi' taken with the editor's suggested 'Qui'; 'licet' read as 'liquet' with the editor. Line 48: 'Ad Maximum... dicens (Epist. 62)' etc. are the edition's references. Line 49: the edition's parenthetical glosses and conjectures (e.g. 'Deum Verbum', 'prava scripta reprobamus') followed; 'Deum vero ejus et personam' read as 'eum vero et ejus personam'. The quotation beginning 'Naturas discernimus Dei Verbi' is garbled in the text and translated as it stands. The subject of 'blanditum fuisse' (Solomon) is supplied. The section number XIX is missing from the edition.

XXII: 'Sic igitur permanere In sanctitate servante constat' is corrupt; rendered conjecturally. 'cujus erga unitatem' refers to Paul. Letter VI is generally regarded as spurious (Pseudo-Isidorian), drawing on Gregory the Great's letters, as the edition's bracketed note indicates; that note is translated in square brackets. XXI: 'imo. tescere' read as 'innotescere'; 'plus in haereticis sensum proprium, quam testatio Eusebii absolvere potuit' is awkward, rendered by sense. 'is in errore petit' read as 'perit'. Several scripture references in the edition are inaccurate (e.g. 1 Cor. 1, 1 Pet. 5 and 3:14).

Line 55: 'ut pontii.' read as 'ut possitis'. Line 57: 'destuuntu' read with the editor's correction 'per se sua dogmata destruunt'; 'certam provinciam' rendered 'a province properly so called'; 'anlversum coelum' read as 'universum coetum' (whole body); 'in torre' read as 'in morte'. The letters (a)–(d) are the edition's footnote marks. This decretal is generally regarded as spurious (Pseudo-Isidorian).

Line 60: 'commodatior' is odd (perhaps 'commendatior'); rendered 'more favourable'. 'quaerite faciem ejus semper' is Ps. 104:4. Line 66: 'Carmensis' read as 'Catinensis' (Catania), as the heading requires. Line 75: 'omnes quae sua quaerunt' lacks a verb (cf. Phil. 2:21, 'omnes quaerunt'); 'dun- Laxat' read as 'duntaxat'; a word is missing before 'ad Deum pertinent' (presumably 'quae'); 'morem' read as 'uxorem' (wife); 'Gatinensem' read as 'Catinensem'. Line 76: 'eo.. cessisse' read as 'concessisse'; 'derectui' as 'defectui'. The servant's name varies: Miscena / Micina. Lines 64 and 76 are two versions of the same text.

Line 79: Constitutus is taken as the priest's personal name, as the repeated 'Constitutus' in the decree requires. Line 83: 'nomine et actu Dei Senum' read as 'Dei Servum' (servant of God in name and deed); possibly a proper name such as Deusdedit or Servusdei is meant. 'meMori consilio' read as 'meliori consilio'. The clause 'sed magis robur eis ac Domini Salvatoris quae omnes canonicos superexaltat libros, auctoritatem praestant' seems corrupt; translated by sense. The letter is a Pseudo-Isidorian forgery, as its placement in the appendix suggests. Editorial variant readings have been omitted; source citations in parentheses have been kept.

Several evident scanning errors have been read silently (e.g. 'eoguut' = cogunt, 'collecta'a' = collectas, 'sini!' = sinit, 'de.,;.. ciet' = despiciet). In 'causam necessitatis aut utilitatis habes et mutare' a word such as 'potestatem' seems to have dropped out; it is supplied in brackets. The stray 'a' before 'spiritus timentium' has been ignored. 'praedicatio offensionis' is probably an error for 'deprecatio offensionis' (Sirach 34:19 in the Vulgate) and has been translated in that sense. The long passage of Ennodius-derived rhetoric (the 'court of heaven ... curule seats' sentences) is obscure in the Latin and has been rendered closely. The closing scriptural catena is from Sirach 34–35.

This letter is generally regarded as a spurious (Pseudo-Isidorian) decretal; the parenthetical source references are the edition's. Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. vicere > vivere, acqui- not > acquirant, luco > fuco, benefidum > beneficium, possi.. > possit). 'sainte prælata' is corrupt; read as 'sancti praelati' (holy prelates). Some Ennodian sentences ('Praebent hominibus...', 'Redit ad mortales...', 'Jam latebat...', 'sopori quietem tribuite') are obscure and the renderings tentative. The year '58i' is read as 581, though the 15th indiction would correspond to December 581/582.

The first two lines are the editor's heading summarising the letter; the trailing 'b' and the 'a' in the preceding heading are footnote marks. 'In Albis paschalibus' refers to Easter week (the week in white garments). 'Apparitio Domini' is Epiphany. 'itas' and 'Etclesia' read as 'Istas' and 'Ecclesia'. The letter is generally regarded as a spurious decretal.

nodes.text: IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 590. POPE PELAGIUS II.
THE LETTERS AND DECREES OF POPE PELAGIUS II.
FIRST LETTER [formerly III],
TO GREGORY THE DEACON
That he should obtain help for him from the emperor against the Lombards.

Bishop Pelagius to his beloved son Gregory the deacon. We have taken care to make known to you everything that was necessary through Honoratus the notary, whom we have sent to your Affection together with our brother and fellow bishop Sebastian. Since he has been in those parts as far as Ravenna until now with the glorious man, the lord Decius the patrician, he will be eager to inform you about everything by his own report, so that if you judge anything necessary, you can put it before the lord emperor. For such great calamities and tribulations have been brought upon us by the treachery of the Lombards, against their own sworn oath, that no one could be equal to recounting them. How we received the aforesaid brother Sebastian, and in what charity he was held among us at your suggestion, you will be able to learn from his own report. He has also promised us to put before our most pious lord the emperor the needs and dangers of all Italy. Speak, then, and consult together on how you can quickly come to the aid of our dangers. For the state is so hard pressed here that, unless God inspires the heart of the most pious prince to bestow on his servants the mercy implanted in him, and to deign to grant, over and above that *diacoposis*, at least one master of the soldiers and one duke, we are left destitute in every distress, since the Roman parts above all seem emptied of every garrison. And the exarch writes that he can provide no remedy for us, since he declares that he is not able to suffice even to guard those parts. May God therefore command him to come swiftly to the aid of our dangers, before the army of that most abominable people succeeds, with God against us (which God forbid), in seizing the places still held by the state. Hasten, with God's help, to send the priest back to us, for he is known to be altogether necessary both in your monastery and in the work over which we have set him. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of October, in the third indiction.
LETTER II [formerly IV],
TO AUNACHARIUS, BISHOP OF AUXERRE

He commends the orthodox faith of the kings of the Franks, and urges him to persuade them not to make a treaty with the Lombards; and on the relics which he sends. To his most beloved brother Aunarius, Pelagius, of the city of Rome
bishop.

We have read the praiseworthy wishes of your Charity, in which you indicate that you would have wished to come to us, had a movement of the heathen not stood in the way. For although we are always, in spirit, both together and one in the Lord, yet we find that both the older fathers and the apostles themselves sought bodily presence too. But while you set out your wishes and the reasons by which you were prevented, we were surprised that you had paid too little attention to what tells against those very excuses. For if you judge this city venerable to the world, if you proclaim that the governance of all the churches is directed toward the peace of the apostolic see, why do you not also groan with compassionate charity over our tribulations and present distresses? You know that we are commanded by the divine mouth through the Apostle (Rom. 13, Gal. 6) to love one another, to bear one another's burdens, and that whenever any of the brothers is burned, we are burned, while almost before your eyes so much innocent blood has been shed, the sacred altars are thus violated, and the catholic faith is thus insulted by idolaters. We know, as you do too, that these are temporal scourges and serve for testing, as we trust in heavenly mercy; and, as you write, our Lord will soon give joy out of tribulation, because those who act wickedly will be destroyed, and the enemies of God, as soon as they are exalted, will vanish like smoke (Ps. 36), and the nations will perish altogether from his land. For this reason it would have befitted you, who there are members of the catholic Church, joined into one body under the governance of one head, to hasten with all the strength you could to our peace and quiet, for the sake of the very unity of the Holy Spirit. For we do not believe it was idle, or arranged without great wonder of divine providence, that your kings are like the Roman empire in the confession of the orthodox faith, except so that [providence] might provide neighbours and helpers to this city, from which [that faith] had arisen, and to all Italy. Take care, then, dearest brother, lest, while the power to help us has been given by God to your kings, your Charity be accused of levity toward us, since you either neglect or postpone urging such things upon them, who are so devoted to your priesthood both in faith and in counsels. The sacred relics which both your Charity and our most glorious son asked to have sent, we have dispatched together with the sanctification attached to them. For this reason we no less admonish you that you hasten, as far as is possible for you, to free from the pollution of the heathen the temples of those whose power you seek; and that you urge your kings most insistently to hasten, with wholesome foresight, to separate themselves from friendship and alliance with the most abominable enemy, the Lombards, lest, when the time of vengeance upon them comes, as we trust through divine mercy it will come quickly, they too be found sharers with them. For it is written that not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are to be punished (Rom. 1). May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the third day before the Nones of October, in the reign of the lord Tiberius Augustus at Constantinople, in the seventh year.
LETTER III [formerly V],
WHICH IS THE FIRST TO ELIAS AND THE BISHOPS OF ISTRIA.
To his most beloved brothers Elias and the other bishops, and to all the sons established in the Church in the parts of Istria, Pelagius, bishop of the holy catholic Church of the city of Rome.

That we are sending our letters to your Affection rather late, dearest brothers and sons, should not be believed to come from ill will, or from dissembling or negligence; rather, as you know, the state of the times and the pressure of the enemy have prevented it until now. For as the Lord says through the prophet: Can a woman forget the son of her womb (Isa. 49)? Let it not be believed, then, that we have not grieved with heavy weeping and groaning at the division of our own innermost parts. But would, dearest ones, that the Lord might enlighten the eyes of your heart, so that you could see the groans of our heart for you. For, as the blessed apostle says (2 Cor. 11), who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn? And elsewhere (1 Cor. 12): Because one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. Now, therefore, that almighty God, for the good fortune of the Christian princes, through the labours and solicitude of our most excellent son Smaragdus, exarch and chartulary of the sacred palace, has deigned to grant us peace and quiet for the time being, we hasten with all solicitude to send the present letter to you, exhorting and beseeching that no one should strive to remain any longer in division from the Church. For we, according to the word of the Gospel, strive, as far as our frailty is able, to show humbly and with sincerity of heart to your Fraternity and Affection what has been commanded us. For you know the Lord proclaiming in the Gospel (Luke 22): Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I have asked the Father for you, that your faith may not fail, and you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.

Consider, dearest ones, that the Truth could not lie, nor could the faith of Peter ever be shaken or changed. For when the devil had demanded all the disciples for sifting, the Lord testifies that he prayed for Peter alone, and willed that the others be strengthened by him. To him also, for the greater love which he showed the Lord beyond the others, the care of feeding the sheep was entrusted; to him he handed the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and upon him he promised that he would build his Church, and testified that the gates of hell would not prevail against it (Matt. 16). But since the enemy of the human race does not cease until the end of the age to sow tares over the good seed in the Lord's Church, therefore, lest perhaps someone, with malicious zeal and at the devil's instigation, should presume to invent and argue something about the integrity of our faith, and your minds should perhaps seem to be disturbed by this, we have judged it necessary through this present letter of ours both to exhort you with tears to return to the bosom of mother Church, and to send you our satisfaction concerning the integrity of our faith, so that no suspicion of us may remain in your hearts, and so that on the day of the divine and fearful judgement I may not be found guilty for my silence.

For we hold the aforesaid faith, and defend it with all purity of conscience even to the shedding of blood, which was handed down by the apostles and kept inviolate by their successors, which the revered synod of Nicaea of three hundred and eighteen Fathers received and set down in the creed; and also [that of] Constantinople of one hundred and fifty Fathers, held under the prince Theodosius the elder of pious memory; also the first [synod] of Ephesus, over which presided our predecessor of blessed memory Celestine, bishop of the city of Rome, and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria; and also [that] of Chalcedon of six hundred and thirty Fathers, which met under the emperor Marcian of pious memory, and over which Pope Leo of holy memory presided through his legates and vicars. And as the opposition of various heresies, which had to be condemned, demanded, they proclaimed the same faith more fully, crying out with one and the same sense. We also venerate in every respect, hold, and defend the letter of the aforesaid Leo of blessed memory addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, which is also called the Tome, and according to its tenor, with the Lord's help, we preach. And just as our often-mentioned predecessor Pope Leo of blessed memory received and confirmed the synod of Chalcedon, so we too, by the working of divine grace, venerate, keep, and defend it in every respect.

But if anyone either thinks, or believes, or presumes to teach against this faith, let him know that, according to the judgement of those same Fathers, he is condemned and anathematized. Do not, then, allow yourselves to be stirred up again by false suspicions or rumours, and to remain in division from the Church through the persuasions of evil men (which may the Lord avert). For why do you divide yourselves from the unity of the holy Church, when you know that nothing new, nothing (God forbid) contrary is preached or held in the said Church? Rather, it is shown in every way that one and the same faith, which is known to have been handed down by the apostles and explained and confirmed by the holy Fathers and the aforesaid four synods, is most sincerely held and defended. Since, then, no question or suspicion can arise for you concerning the firmness of the faith, [be pleased] to remain in the unity of the faith and in the bosom of holy mother, the catholic and apostolic Church. If perhaps there is some cause by which your minds seem to have been made to stumble, remain in the charity of unity and choose from among our brothers and sons those whom you should send to us to inquire into the things by which you are troubled; and we are ready, according to the apostolic precept (1 Pet. 3), both to receive them with charity and to render with humility an account to the satisfaction [of what pleases you]; and, when they wish to return, to send them back with all affection and with most sincere goodwill, without any hindrance.

Let us hear, moreover, the Teacher of the Gentiles crying out: As you have received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and confirmed in the faith, as you have learned, abounding in thanksgiving. See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit; and let your zeal no longer be turned to contention or superfluous questions (Col. 2). Attend with humility of heart to the voice of the same apostle; for writing to Timothy he says thus: But avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they breed quarrels; and a servant of the Lord must not quarrel (2 Tim. 2); and again to the Corinthians: But if anyone among you seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God (1 Cor. 11); and again, after other things: God is not [a God] of dissension, but of peace.

Consider, then, that whoever is not in the peace and unity of the Church cannot have the Lord. Likewise, writing to the Galatians, he says: Those who are of faith, these are the sons of Abraham (Gal. 3). And the Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the Gentiles by faith, announced beforehand to Abraham: In you all nations shall be blessed (Gen. 22). Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham. What excuse, then, can you have any longer before the Lord after this present satisfaction of ours, when no contrary suspicion will remain for you concerning the sincerity and purity of our faith? Hear the same apostle with authority also admonishing: Do not be led astray; bad conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15). Let us not, then, be outwitted by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his designs. With brotherly love, then, and humility pleasing to God, if anyone's mind perhaps seems to be made to stumble in some matter, let him, remaining in the charity of unity, inquire and find out. For as the blessed apostle James says: Where there is jealousy and contention, there is also instability and every evil work (James 3); and again the Teacher of the Gentiles: Who hindered you from obeying charity? This persuasion is not from him who called you; a little leaven corrupts the whole lump (Gal. 5); and elsewhere: I am confident in the Lord that you will think nothing else; but he who troubles you will bear judgement, whoever he is (ibid.); and in what follows he says: Would that those who trouble you were cut off (ibid.)! And again, admonishing, he says: But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another (ibid.); and again: If we live by the spirit, let us also walk by the spirit; let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another, envying one another. Let us bear one another's burdens, and so we shall fulfil the law of Christ (ibid.); and elsewhere the same apostle says: I bend my knees to the Lord, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, power to be strengthened through his Spirit in the inner man, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, rooted and grounded in charity, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints (Eph. 3). And after other things: I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling with which you have been called, with all humility and meekness, with patience, bearing with one another in charity, eager to keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all (Eph. 4). And since we have such apostolic exhortations, who will separate us from the charity that is in Christ Jesus our Lord? For if we attend diligently with humility and weeping, we consider and understand that he is our ambusher of whom it is said: For your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5); whom, according to the exhortation of the same apostle, we must resist and oppose with all concord and unity in the strength of faith. For we have all learned by example, dearest brothers and sons, how great evils and how great scourges have followed upon the division of the Church. Hence we trust in his mercy, though unworthy, that if he grants that his Church be united and brought to peace, all the scourges which we have received for our sins will be removed from us more swiftly, and the unity and firmness of the Church's peace will obtain for us peace both temporal and eternal.

Only we ask, and beseech, and adjure you by the divine and fearful judgement of God, where no man will be able to help himself by arguments or excuses, that the Church of God be no longer divided through you, but that we may possess and hold the inheritance of the Lord with common zeal. And what his inheritance is, let us hear from his own words spoken to the disciples: My peace I give you, my peace I leave you (John 14); and again: By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another (John 13). Let us all, as the Vessel of election says, say the same thing, and let there be no schisms among you, but let us be perfect in the same mind and in the same knowledge (1 Cor. 1), so that, gathered into the bosom of mother Church, we may become one flock, and under the keeping of the one shepherd Christ may be preserved unharmed by his protection and defence from all the snares of the enemy, external and internal. We have sent these things to you through our brother and fellow bishop Redemptus and Quodvultdeus, abbot of the monastery of the greater basilica of the blessed apostle Peter; may your Affection receive them with a charity pleasing to God, and let them return to us without delay with the joy of your unity, so that, knowing the love and obedience of your Charity, we may deserve to say together and truly with the holy angels: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will (Luke 2).
LETTER IV [formerly VI]
WHICH IS THE SECOND TO THE BISHOPS OF ISTRIA.
To his most beloved brothers Elias and the other bishops of Istria, Pelagius, bishop.

We have received the letter of your Affection through those whom you sent, and on reading it through we were struck with heavy grief and sorrow; for you neither answered what we wrote to you, nor, as brotherly charity would have befitted, having accepted the satisfaction concerning our faith, did you yield obedience by returning to the unity of the Church; finally, you did not even allow those who came to be sent otherwise than that they should not suffer themselves to accept a most open and most clear satisfaction; but they showed us in writing a sort of capitulary, or rather an interdict, asserting that nothing else had been enjoined on them by you except that they should merely be the bearers of your letter. In it, however, you are read to have sought no satisfaction of reason, but [it was] as though it had set out for us something already judged; and how perverse this is, how unjust, and how hostile to the rules of the Fathers, you can learn most brilliantly with divine help, if you are willing to approach the knowledge of the truth. Hence it befits us to cry out tearfully with the prophet: I was dumb, and was humbled, and kept silent from good things, and the sorrow of my heart was renewed (Ps. 38). The sorrow of our heart was renewed when the scandal of long division is by no means overcome by so great a splendour of faith, especially because, deceived by the persuasion of perverse men, you have sent us writings infected with various contagions; and because you attempted to insert from the letters of the Fathers certain testimonies not only unsuitable but not even pertaining to the case, so that you did not even keep the order of the testimonies as it is in the letters of the Fathers themselves, inasmuch as what had been written under the name of one was brought forward under the title of another's name. In this the apostolic saying evidently fits you: Understanding neither what they say nor about what they make assertions (1 Tim. 1).

This indeed we believe is not to be ascribed to your malice or cunning, but we perceive it to have been devised by the venom of the most malignant enemy, who does not rest from sowing tares in the Church of God through vessels of wrath until the end of the age. From this we understand that your Fraternity has not read the letters from which you set down testimonies; for if their writing were known to you, you would not pretend that those things which were most plainly set down solely for the cause of the faith fit other matters. For this reason I exhort and desire that you be recalled more quickly from the error of division into which you have fallen through false opinions, and that you not (as it is written) bear a yoke with unbelievers (2 Cor. 6), but submit gentle necks again to that yoke of which the Lord himself says: For my yoke is sweet, and my burden is light (Matt. 11). This no one will in any way be able either to bear or to learn, unless he has been yoked to that same yoke by the bonds of charity, and has through love submitted mind, shoulders and strength to that burden, as to a spiritual load. For just as the animosity of separation binds the understanding through pride, so the humility of recovered charity enlightens minds, persevering in the unity of faith, unto the knowledge of the truth.

For this reason, to the bearers of the present letter, whom your Fraternity sent, certain things were read out again both from the codices and from the ancient registers of the archive of the holy apostolic see, by which it plainly appears that nothing of what you set down in your letter concerning the cause of the Three Chapters fits in any way, or can plausibly be adapted to it. Therefore it is necessary that you all read through the synodal letters carefully and attentively, so that you may recognise more clearly that the holy Fathers confirmed nothing else concerning the synod of Chalcedon in their letters except that the definition of the faith should be kept inviolable. For our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Leo, writing to confirm that same synod, says among other things: "So that it may not, through malicious interpreters, seem doubtful whether I have approved what was established concerning the faith in the synod of Chalcedon by your unanimity, I have sent these writings to all our brothers and fellow bishops who were present at the said council, which the most glorious and most clement prince, as I have asked, will deign to bring to your notice for love of the catholic faith; so that both the brotherhood at large and the hearts of all the faithful may know that I have strengthened my own judgement together with you, not only through the brothers who acted in my place, but also by approving the synodal acts: namely, in the cause of the faith alone (which must often be said), on account of which it pleased [all] that a general council be assembled, both by the command of the most Christian princes and with the consent of the apostolic see." [Thus far the words of Saint Leo.]

But lest perhaps some question or doubt should still seem to remain in your minds, we have likewise taken care to point out more openly what he wrote to Maximus, bishop of the Church of Antioch. After many things he speaks thus: "If indeed anything is reported to have been done by those brothers whom I sent to the holy synod in my place, beyond what pertained to the cause of the faith, it will have no validity; for they were sent by the apostolic see only for this, that, heresies being cut off, they should be defenders of the catholic faith. For whatever is brought to episcopal examination beyond the special matters of synodal councils may admit of being judged," etc. Behold, as was said above, you know, dearest brothers, that our oft-mentioned predecessor confirmed nothing else than what was defined concerning the firmness of the faith, which you can learn more fully, if you wish, in nearly all his letters. For the private cases which were dealt with there after the definition of the faith, he not only did not confirm, but even permitted them to be reconsidered and judged afresh. As for the Encyclia (which is a collection of episcopal letters, from which you likewise set down some testimonies unsuitably in your writings), from what source the case arose, or what the emperor Leo of pious memory wrote to the bishops throughout all the provinces in consulting them, or how he received replies from them, you will be able, even if we keep silent, to be more fully informed by reading them, so that henceforth no contrivance of malicious perversity may find room for stealing into your hearts. For on account of the length of this letter we have declined to set out the course of that case. For if, with zeal of charity and with the fear of the Lord, you carefully and attentively reread what is written by us, you will easily perceive how great a danger it is to be separated so long from the universal Church for the sake of superfluous questions and the defence of heretical chapters.

Do not then, out of love of boasting, which is always very close to pride, remain in the vice of obstinacy, since on the day of judgement none of you will be able to excuse himself, and neither Theodore of Mopsuestia nor the letter of Ibas, which was brought forward by the opponents, will be able to help you before the tribunal of so great a Judge. Let us therefore obey the Teacher of the Gentiles, who says in the first letter to the Corinthians: Strive for the better gifts, and I show you a still more excellent way (1 Cor. 12). What, then, are the greater things which he promises to show, let us hear more attentively from his own voice: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, and if I distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing (ibid. 13); and again: Faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greater of these is charity (ibid.). What confidence, then, will you be able to have before the Lord, when, seeing that no scandal arises for you from the integrity of our faith, you persist for so long in being divided through superfluous questions from the Church of God, which is one, and from brotherly charity? For where the Church is established, although it is made plain by the voice of the Lord himself in the holy Gospel, let us nevertheless hear what blessed Augustine, mindful of that same saying of the Lord, has defined. For he says that the Church of God is established in those who are known to preside over the apostolic sees through the succession of bishops; and whoever cuts himself off from the communion or authority of those sees is shown to be in schism. And after other things: Placed outside, even if you die for the name of Christ, [you will not be counted] among the members of Christ. Suffer for Christ while clinging to the body; fight for the head. And blessed Cyprian, the distinguished martyr, in the book which he entitled with the name of unity, says among other things: The beginning proceeds from unity; and the primacy is given to Peter, so that the one Church and chair of Christ may be shown; and all are shepherds, but the flock is shown to be one, which is fed by the apostles in unanimous agreement. And shortly after: Does he who does not hold this unity of the Church believe that he holds the faith? Does he who deserts and resists the chair of Peter, on which the Church is founded, trust that he is in the Church? Likewise after other things: They cannot attain the reward of peace, because they have broken the peace of the Lord with the fury of discord.

Likewise from the same book he says thus: Those who come to the sacrifice with dissension he calls back from the altar, and commands them first to be reconciled with their brother, and then, returning in peace, to offer their gift to the Lord (Matt. 5); for God did not look upon Cain's gifts either (Gen. 4); for he could not have the Lord at peace with him who, through the discord of jealousy, did not have peace with his brother. What peace, then, do the enemies of the brothers promise themselves? What sacrifices do the rivals of the priests believe they celebrate? Do those who are gathered outside the Church think that Christ is with them when they are gathered? Such men, even if they are killed in confession of the Name, that stain is not washed away even by blood. The inexpiable and grave guilt of discord is not purged even by suffering. He cannot be a martyr who is not in the Church; he will not be able to reach the kingdom who has forsaken her who is to reign. And after other things: Those cannot abide with God who have refused to be of one mind in the Church of God; though they burn, handed over to flames and fires, or lay down their lives thrown to the beasts, that will not be the crown of faith but the punishment of faithlessness, nor the glorious end of religious virtue but the death of despair: such a man can be killed; he cannot be crowned.

Likewise from the same: Does he think himself to be with Christ, who acts against the priests of Christ? who separates himself from the fellowship of his clergy and people? He bears arms against God, he fights against God's ordinance: an enemy of the altar, a rebel against the sacrifice of Christ, faithless instead of faithful, sacrilegious instead of religious, a disobedient servant, an impious son, a hostile brother, he dares, despising the bishops and forsaking the priests of God, to set up another altar. Likewise the same as above: The crime of schism is worse than that of those who sacrificed, who nevertheless, placed in penance for their crime, entreat the Lord with full satisfactions. Here the Church is sought and entreated; there the Church is fought against. Here there may have been compulsion; there the will is held fast in wickedness. Here he who lapsed harmed only himself; there he who tries to make heresy or schism has deceived many by drawing them with him. Here is the loss of one soul; there the peril of many. Certainly this one understands that he has sinned and laments; that one, swelling in his sin and pleased with his very delights, separates sons from their mother, entices sheep from their shepherd, disturbs the sacraments of God; and whereas the lapsed sinned once, he sins daily. Finally, the lapsed, if he afterwards attains martyrdom, can receive the promises of the kingdom; the other, if he is killed outside the Church, cannot attain the rewards of the Church.

Likewise the same as above: But if in the holy Scriptures discipline is commanded often and everywhere, and the foundation of religion proceeds from the observance and fear of faith, what should we more eagerly seek, what should we more wish for and hold to, than that, with our roots fixed more firmly and our dwellings made solid upon the mass of the strong rock, we should stand unshaken against the storms and whirlwinds of the world, so that through the divine precepts we may be able to come to the gifts of God?

And therefore we exhort and beseech your Affection that, knowing such terrible testimonies of the Fathers, you in no way allow yourselves to persist any longer in the division of the Church, but hasten with the whole intent of your minds to return into the bosom of the holy catholic and apostolic mother, so that, rooted and grounded in the charity of unity, we may be worthy to say: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity (Ps. 132), truly crying out: Our mouth is filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation (Ps. 125). Having answered you in a briefer style indeed, but with abundant charity, we trust both in the minds of your Fraternity and in the power of the divine mercy that you will without doubt be quickly restored to the holy Church. If, however, because of our sins, the enemy of souls should still bring upon you any obstinacy (which God forbid) or doubt, then, in accordance with what the final part of our ruling in the proceedings held before us contains, and as we have taken care to petition our most excellent lord and son Smaragdus, exarch of Italy, hasten to send here to us instructed persons, with whom an account may more easily be given and received, so that no doubt or delay in your agreement may thereafter remain, if full satisfaction is given to them. Or if you are afraid because of the distance of the places or the nature of the times, let an assembly of bishops be held there at Ravenna, to which we too, by God's favour, will send men to be present in our place, from whom you may receive the fullest satisfaction; so that simple souls may no longer remain divided from the holy Church in such long obstinacy over superfluous questions, and so that the sheep wandering from the folds of the Church may not, through you, who ought to be shepherds of the Lord's flock, be devoured by the teeth of the rapacious wolf.
LETTER 5 [formerly 7],
WHICH IS THE THIRD TO ELIAS AND THE BISHOPS OF ISTRIA.

Blessed Gregory mentions this letter in Book II, Letter 36, to the bishops of Ireland, where he calls it a book. Paul Warnefrid, in Book III of the History of the Lombards, chapter 10 (otherwise 20), testifies that it was written by the same blessed Gregory, while he was still a deacon, in the name of Pope Pelagius.
To our most beloved brothers, Elias and all the bishops established in the regions of Istria, Pelagius, bishop.

I. Charity, the mother of virtues (1 Cor. 13), which serves the gains of its Redeemer and never seeks its own, some time ago drove me with panting desire to send your Fraternity writings full of sweetness, which might join to their own body the members of Christ long separated. In them, speaking more with entreaties than with admonitions, I took care to exhort you with all the affection I could, that your Affection should send here those whom you foresaw to be fit for discussing the reasoning, so that in the matter of the Three Chapters they might either learn the things that are plain, or, whatever perhaps seemed obscure, this conference of peaceable intent might open to them. At last I have received the letters of your Affection, which did not seek the grounds of reason but dictated a sentence of judgement already decided among you. This, however, which I see you presume to do on the strength of your own wisdom, I confess I wonder at with sorrow; and yet in my letters, I believe, I showed examples of humility and gave a token of love. But since I have found that the words of my admonition achieve nothing with you, weeping and groaning I am compelled to cry out with the prophet: We have treated Babylon, and she is not healed (Jer. 51). I kindled the fire of charity as much as I could, and wished to burn away the rust of so great a schism; but, as our sins demanded, I have found fulfilled the saying of the prophet, who says: In vain has the smelter smelted; its dross has not been consumed (Jer. 6). No flame of charity is seen in your replies; even after my example they give off no sweetness in all their words; nothing in them sounds of what leads to peace. Consider, I beg you, this (which I cannot say without sobs interrupting me): with what coldness of mind your Fraternity has grown numb through long habit of division, since it does not grow warm again even when rubbed. What then shall I do in all this, except turn to tears for you? For since the roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5), I know that you too, standing outside the sheepfold, [are to be devoured]. I see you as branches not pruned by the removal of fruit, but cut off from the root of the vine. And I see you sweating as workers, yet I know that you labour outside the vineyard. Behold, with the end pressing on, all things are laid waste, the earth is reduced to desolation, and (so to speak) the storm of the flood overwhelms the world, and your Fraternity flees the ark. With Jeremiah I say: Who will give water to my head, and to my eyes a fountain of tears? (Jer. 9) and again: Let our eyes shed tears, and our eyelids flow with waters (ibid.); I will say with him again: I will weep and be at rest. For since I do not find the rest of concord in your hearts, I lay down tears for my weary mind. For what rest can there be for my spirit, if the wound inflicted by the hidden enemy cannot be healed? Behold, in all parts of the world the holy and universal Church shines with the rays of its unity, and yet it still bears the shadow of your division. Everywhere it endures in the state of faith; but the wound it suffers from your cutting off forbids it to rejoice in its own health. For the head does not rejoice in its soundness while the arms are grieving; nor is the breast glad as though unharmed when it is touched by the pains of the inner parts beneath it; for the whole framework of the body is affected if even its outermost part is torn. Whatever, therefore, one part feels another suffering, the harmony of charity draws into itself, as Paul attests, who says: And if one member suffers, the other members suffer with it (1 Cor. 12). We, then, are the ones who are pierced by your pain; we are the ones who are wasted by your schisms. Therefore we ought to come to the aid of your losses with consolation all the more swiftly, the more we are compelled through charity to feel them as our own. For even if we perhaps wished to delay, we are terrified by the voice of heavenly rebuke, which, rebuking slothful shepherds, says: What was broken you have not bound up, and what was cast away you have not brought back, and what was lost you have not sought. If we wish to delay, we are rebuked by the reproach of the Lord, who says through the prophet: Is there no resin in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why then is the wound of the daughter of my people not closed over? (Ezek. 34). For what is meant by resin, which is fuel for fire, and which also joins separated marbles together for the adornment of a house, but charity? It both kindles hearts in love and, so that it may array the holy Church with the adornment of unity, binds together the discordant minds of men through zeal for peace within itself. What is meant by Gilead, which is interpreted 'heap of testimony', but the height of holy Scripture, with its countless mass of sayings? What by the word 'physician', but each preacher? What by the daughter's wound not closed over, but that the guilt of the people is shown naked before the eyes of God? Resin, therefore, is proved to have been lacking in Gilead if, though so many testimonies of holy Scripture are at hand to show the truth, charity of fitting ardour is in no way shown in joining you to the holy Church; and, as though the physician were absent, the wound is not closed over if, when exhortation ceases, the guilt of so great a schism is not covered by any veil of ensuing peace. But it is now time for us to touch the very wounds of your suspicions, and, with God's help, to apply to them the remedies of revealed truth.

II. Your Fraternity suspects, on account of the things done in the times of the emperor Justinian of pious memory, that the holy synod of Chalcedon has been overthrown. But far be this from Christian deed and from Christian thought. For in it the synods of Nicaea, Constantinople and the first of Ephesus were confirmed; and whoever strives to overthrow it in any part is undoubtedly trying to destroy utterly those which were confirmed through it. To this suspicion you add in your writings testimonies from the letters of our holy predecessor Leo and from the Encyclia, to show that the aforesaid holy synod of Chalcedon ought to be kept intact. These, most dear brothers, taken from a few letters, you have set down in a mixed and confused order, so that, while another letter is inserted and one returns to other words of the earlier letter, they might seem to be drawn from many letters. And we wonder greatly why your Fraternity has taken not a few things from (as we have said) so few letters, when it is established that, concerning the intact veneration of the holy synod of Chalcedon, both the countless assertions of our predecessors and the agreement of many Fathers in the Encyclia have poured themselves upon us like a light to the world. But since the order of composition is always joined to itself with such connection that what precedes serves what follows, and what follows depends on what precedes, we shall better make plain the sense of the passages you have cited if, reading below and above, we show either where they tend or on what they depend.

III. The first testimony set down by your Affection, then, is from our holy predecessor Leo, found in his last letter (Letter 78 to the emperor Leo), where he says: 'Concerning the matters defined at Nicaea and at Chalcedon as it pleased God, we dare enter into no discussion, as though those things were doubtful or weak which [are upheld] by such great authority through the Holy Spirit.' (To this you add a second testimony from that letter, found there a little above, where it says: 'Because, as you have said holily and truly, perfection admits no increase, and fullness no addition.') Then, after two testimonies inserted from the Encyclia, your writing repeats words of our aforesaid predecessor Leo, again to the emperor Leo, in which it is said: 'To wish to disturb lawful constitutions inspired by God is the act not of a peaceable man but of a rebel, as the apostle says: To contend with words is useful for nothing but the subversion of the hearers (2 Tim. 2). For if it were always free to dispute by human persuasions, there could never be lacking those who would dare to resist the truth.' (And again, his words to the same: 'Do not allow contests already extinguished to rise up with revived movements against the triumphs of the right hand of almighty God.') A little after, you added a further testimony of his: 'Let nothing at all of what has been well settled be reopened.' The last testimony you set down is contained in his earlier letter, from which many testimonies had already been brought forward, where it is said: 'To seek what has already been made plain, to reopen what has been completed, and to tear up what has been defined, what else is it but to return no thanks for what has been obtained, and to stretch out the wicked appetites of deadly desire toward the food of the forbidden tree?' These, most beloved brothers, are the words of blessed Leo to the emperor Leo that you have set down; and they were plainly brought forward by him for the safeguarding of the inviolate faith, not for the particular cases of bishops that were dealt with at Chalcedon. For that he spoke only for the unblemished observance of the faith must be weighed from what he said earlier in the same letter; for he says, speaking to the same emperor: 'Beyond the care of temporal affairs you perseveringly devote the service of religious providence to divine and eternal ordinances, namely that the catholic faith, which alone gives life to the human race and alone sanctifies it, may remain in one confession, and that the dissensions which arise from the variety of earthly opinions may be driven away from the solidity of that rock upon which the city of God is built.' (If, then, most dear brothers, you did not see the faith flourishing in one solid state in all parts of the world, you would rightly say that something of the holy synod of Chalcedon had been overturned. But since nothing else is now at issue except persons, and you raise no question about the faith of the holy synod of Chalcedon, you have turned aside while seeming to follow the authority of the Fathers. For in order to show with what intention he had said these things, when blessed Leo declared that what has been completed ought not to be reopened, he at once added: 'Because you deign to look with more anxious care to the peace of the universal Church and to the safeguarding of the catholic faith.' Why, then, when he forbade the defined things to be torn up, did he at once add an admonition about safeguarding the catholic faith, unless to show that he had said this not about reopening particular cases but only about the profession of faith? For the very matters now turning in your question are those which our predecessor blessed Leo himself also judges, since he confirms only what was decreed at Chalcedon concerning the faith. For writing to Anatolius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, when he rebuked him for a certain new presumption, he says (Letter 58): 'That you should drag the holy synod, assembled by the zeal of the most Christian emperor solely to extinguish heresy and to confirm the catholic faith, into an occasion for ambition.' (And again: 'He wished so to abuse the synodal council that he might either lead astray by corrupting, or compel by terrifying, into agreeing with him the brothers who had been called together only on the business of the faith and had discharged the definition of that matter which needed attending to.') And to show that he accepted absolutely nothing from the synod of Chalcedon except what had been done concerning the faith alone, he says, writing to that same synod (Letter 61): 'So that both the brotherly community and the hearts of all the faithful may know that I have joined my own judgement with you, not only through the brothers who acted in my place, but also through approval of the synodal proceedings, namely in the cause of the faith alone, which must often be said.' (He, then, who agreed with the synod of Chalcedon, convened for the cause of faith alone, only in that, without doubt shows himself a stranger to all the things that were done there in particular. Hence again, writing to the aforesaid Anatolius about receiving the presbyter Atticus, he says (Letter 77): 'So that he may profess that he will keep in all respects the definition of the synod of Chalcedon concerning the faith, to which your Affection also consented by subscribing, and which the authority of the apostolic see confirmed.') In speaking of the definition of the synod of Chalcedon he would not have watchfully added 'concerning the faith', unless he had rejected the cases that had been raised there in particular (yet he would have excepted only the one which singularly displeased him). But since he accepted nothing of the synod except the definition of faith, what else is this but that he refused the other things which were raised there in particular? Nor, if he had wished, would he have feared to censure only one cause of the aforesaid Anatolius, since he did not fear to make known by letters sent around, both to the most serene emperors and to its author, that same Anatolius, that it was not approved by his judgement. Since, however, he speaks privately to the aforesaid Anatolius about that matter, and again, writing to the synod, confesses that he accepts what had been done concerning the faith alone, it is clear both that he rebuked Anatolius for the particular cause of the offence, and that he permitted all the private business that had been raised in the synod to be reopened.

IV. Again, in your writing a testimony and example is set down from the Encyclia, where many bishops say together: 'We can neither disturb nor change one iota or tittle of what was decreed at Chalcedon.' (To this you also added another testimony, as though from the same letter, which is undoubtedly that of Anatolius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, where he says: 'But concerning the holy synod of Chalcedon I say that even to question it at all, or to turn over again anything of what was defined by it, is the act of men who only lie in wait against the Churches and the universal peace of Christ.') In what respect he forbids it to be turned over and torn up, he himself adds; for he says: 'Since the apostolic and paternal doctrines long ago handed down to us were strengthened and confirmed in it.' (If, then, it is the act of men who lie in wait to tear up the apostolic and paternal doctrines, it is beyond doubt clear that those who receive those same paternal and apostolic doctrines intact are not men who lie in wait. For by God's help we hold the faith of that same synod unblemished, and we so pass over, with our holy predecessor Leo, the private business that was done there, that we keep the definition of faith set forth there even with death set before us. In the preceding testimony of many bishops together, however, we do not know whether the composer or the copyist erred; for it is not contained in the Encyclia as you have set it down in your writings, but thus: 'For we can neither disturb nor violate one iota or tittle of what was rightly and inviolably defined by it.') But it is one thing that what was decreed cannot be disturbed, and quite another that what was rightly and blamelessly decreed cannot be disturbed. For those most learned men knew that the things done there concerning particular cases had by no means been accepted by our predecessor Leo; and therefore they write most cautiously that what was rightly and blamelessly defined by it ought not to be disturbed or violated, lest, if they said they confirmed everything, they should run against the judgement of our often-mentioned predecessor Leo. Hence they also at once add: 'Let us always think as the Church of the apostolic see of the Romans thinks.')

V. After these examples you also set down a testimony of the same predecessor of ours Leo to bishop Basil, where he says: 'I beseech your Affection that you relax your mind in nothing from the definitions of the synod of Chalcedon, and suffer what was composed by divine inspiration to be violated by no novelty' (and again: 'But so that this exhortation may come to the knowledge of all the brothers and fellow bishops, let the care of your Fraternity diligently see to it, since (as must often be said) the whole Christian religion is thrown into confusion if anything of what was decreed at Chalcedon is torn up.') But whether he asserts this of the particular cases of certain persons or of the definition of the holy faith, let it be asked what he himself says above; for he says: 'I have sent these writings, by which I believed your Affection should be admonished to resist wicked presumptions with holy constancy, lest our common faith be found in anyone either fearful or lukewarm.' (He, then, who put first an admonition to keep the faith showed in what respect he wished the synod to be guarded. But if we are in doubt about the words of this letter, let us seek from his other letters in what sense he said these things. For sending his writings concerning that same synod to Marcian Augustus, he says (Letter 59): 'I have sent writings to your Glory and to the bishop of Constantinople which plainly show that I approve what had been defined concerning the catholic faith in the aforesaid synod.') If he accepted all the particular cases of the same synod too, why does he specifically assert that he approves what was defined concerning the catholic faith in the aforesaid synod? Again, writing to the aforesaid emperor: 'Since your Piety and most religious will must be obeyed in every way, I have gladly added my judgement to the synodal constitutions which pleased me concerning the confirmation of the catholic faith.' (If, then, he affirms that the confirmation of the catholic faith pleased him and that he added his judgement to it, it is clear that in those things in which there was no confirmation of the faith he did not add his judgement.

VI. Moreover you also insert in your writings a testimony from a letter of the same blessed Leo, which he addresses to Basil: 'We must act piously and steadfastly, lest, while a dispute of such men is admitted, the authority of what has been divinely defined be diminished.' And below: 'For what has been fully defined is not to be called back into any dispute, lest at the will of the condemned we ourselves should seem to be in doubt about things which plainly agree in every respect with the prophetic, evangelical and apostolic authorities.' (But what he asserts to have been 'divinely defined' above, or 'fully defined' below, let your Fraternity weigh from this letter itself or from his other letters, in which he never recalls the particular proceedings, but confirms only what was set forth concerning the faith. Hence in these words too it is watchfully expressed, and it is shown what he called 'fully defined', when he says: 'lest we should seem to be in doubt about those very things which plainly agree in every respect with the prophetic, evangelical and apostolic authorities.') Weigh, I beg you, dearest brothers, whether the writings of Theodore agree with the prophetic, evangelical and apostolic authorities, which with wicked daring deny that our Redeemer is Lord. Weigh whether that letter seems to agree with the prophetic, evangelical and apostolic authorities, in which both Nestorius, the enemy of the Church, is defended, and Cyril, the defender of the Church, is accused. Weigh whether those writings of Theodoret agree with the prophetic, evangelical and apostolic authorities, which, first published against the right faith, he himself afterwards, when converted, condemned. You also set down last a testimony of the often-mentioned Leo to the presbyter Aetius, in which he says: 'Let him not allow a contest to be brought over matters laid to rest, whoever reopens which is found to be sacrilegious, not playful.' (Concerning what matters he asserts this, he himself makes plain when writing to the same Aetius, saying: 'I shall never be able to think anything different from the apostolic [teachings], nor to depart from my own judgement; nor would I alter by any variation what I confessed by the revelation of the Holy Spirit and what I made known with the whole synod proclaiming it with me in its profession; since it would be easier for me to be taken from this world by any tortures whatever than to be changed from the profession which I have believed in common [with all].') If, then, the whole matter which must not be reopened is solely the profession of faith, he will be the sacrilegious reopener of matters who departs from its profession. For that the same blessed Leo guards with the greatest zeal only the profession of faith in the synod, he shows in countless letters, from which we briefly touch on a few, so that your Fraternity, made more certain by them, may gather how much we leave unsaid. For this is why he addresses Marcian Augustus in his writing, saying (Letter 59): 'Let your Clemency know that I have specially delegated this to my brother, bishop Julian, that whatever he finds there to pertain to the guarding of the faith, he should confidently suggest to your Power in my name.' (This is why, writing to Pulcheria Augusta, he says (Letter 60): 'As for the most pious emperor's wish that I should send writings to all the bishops who were present at the synod of Chalcedon, by which I should confirm what was defined there concerning the rule of faith, I have gladly fulfilled it.') This is why, writing to bishop Julian, he says: 'What the most clement emperor thought necessary I have gladly fulfilled, namely to send writings to all the brothers who were present at the synod of Chalcedon, by which I should show that what was confirmed by our holy brothers concerning the rule of faith pleased me.' (This is why, writing again to Pulcheria Augusta, he says (Letter 58): 'How far your Worthiness ought to trust my brother, your venerator, bishop Julian, judge by the judgement of the apostolic see, since in the cause of the faith, which your glorious Piety serves, I have delegated my place to him to this extent, that, not departing from the deference owed to you, he should not cease to represent me to your Piety.') For in mentioning the cause of the faith he would by no means have said 'to this extent', unless he had wished whatever was done outside the faith to be excluded from the synod.

VII. Again, it is said in your letter that you were taught by the apostolic see, and confirmed by the archive of the holy Church over which by God's authority we preside, that you ought not to consent to this matter which was done under the emperor Justinian of pious memory; and you add this support to your excuse, saying that at the beginning of the case both the apostolic see, through Pope Vigilius, and all the leading men of the Latin provinces strongly resisted the condemnation of the Three Chapters. In these words we observe that the very thing which ought to have drawn you to consent pulls you away from consent. For Latin men, ignorant of Greek, not knowing the language, came late to recognise the error; and they ought to be believed all the more readily, in that their steadfastness did not rest from the contest until they recognised the truth. Your Fraternity would rightly despise their consent if with headlong daring they had consented before they recognised the truth; but since they laboured long, and for a long time contended even to the point of injuries, let your Fraternity weigh from this that they would not suddenly abandon so many labours unless they had recognised what is true. For what divine counsel do we believe there was, brothers, in almighty God's long permitting Saul to be an opponent of his faith, and then making him a preacher of his faith, except to show to all to whom he was to preach through him that the Gospel of God is very true, since it was preached by such hardness brought low, so that his hearers, recalling what he had done against the faithful, should perceive that he had suddenly turned to the faith not without evident reason? Hence he himself too, when telling the Lord that his preaching ought easily to be received by unbelievers, says: 'Lord, they themselves know that I was shutting up in prison and beating throughout the synagogues those who believed in you' (Acts 22). And when he saw that the Galatians, having abandoned the rule of the Gospel, had turned aside into the error of Judaism, he recounted to them his own former hardness against the Gospel, and turned their minds back from their faithless purpose, saying: 'You have heard of my former conduct in Judaism, how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and was laying it waste; and I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my nation, being more abundantly a zealot for the traditions of my fathers. But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother's womb, and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately confer with flesh and blood.' See, dearest brothers, Paul, the eminent teacher, because he long resisted the truth, drew from this a support for confirming the hearts of his hearers in the preaching of that same truth: showing indeed that the faith which he had earlier resisted with so much effort he afterwards did not hold without the certainty of great reason.

VIII. Your Affection ought therefore to consider that the consent of our predecessors in this case was the less empty afterwards, the more it had first sweated in the hard labours of contradiction. But beyond this let your Fraternity call to mind the deed of Peter, who surpasses even Paul. For he long resisted the holy Church receiving the Gentiles to the faith without circumcision, and long withdrew himself from communion with the converted Gentiles, as Paul attests, who says: 'When he had come to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy. For before certain men came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they had come, he withdrew himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision' (Galatians 1). And a little later: 'And when I saw that he was not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before all: If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?' Yet he, having afterwards accepted the reasoning from the same Paul, when he saw certain men burdening the Gentiles coming to the Church with the weight of keeping circumcision, says: 'Why do you tempt God, placing on the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?' (Acts 15). Ought Peter, the prince of the apostles, teaching things unlike himself, to have been answered at these words, most chosen brothers: 'We cannot listen to what you say, because you preached something else before'? If, then, in the business of the Three Chapters one thing was said while the truth was being sought, and another when the truth had been found, why is a change of judgement charged as a crime against this see, which is humbly venerated by the whole Church in its founder? For it is not a change of judgement but inconstancy of mind that is at fault. When, therefore, the intention remains unchangeable towards knowledge of what is right, what hinders if, abandoning its ignorance, it changes its words? Of God himself too, the author of all, we know by the testimony of Scripture that, while his counsel remains [unchanged], he often changes his judgement; for no unforeseen outcome had befallen him when he said of the one whom he himself had commanded to be anointed: 'I repent that I anointed Saul king in Israel' (1 Kings 15). For he foreknew that he would do this even then, when he preferred him as though approving him; nor did grief come upon him as unforeseen, so as to lead to repentance; yet he intimates that he repents, because, without changing his counsel, he changes the words he had formerly spoken about him.

IX. But to the testimonies you set out from the letters of Leo our predecessor, you prefixed these words: 'It is the teaching of your reverend see, through blessed Leo and his successors, from whom we have presumed to recall a few things, that a dead man ought by no means to be condemned by men'; (and yet you added no testimonies of his by which you might establish this judgement. For what you appended forbids the faith to be reconsidered, but does not deny that the faithless dead may be condemned. Nor do we recall that blessed Leo our predecessor said this anywhere. And who does not know that the preaching of this same Leo and of blessed Augustine in no way contradict each other? For Augustine, writing to Count Boniface, says (Letter 50, above, collation 5): 'If the charges they brought against Caecilian were true, and could at some time be shown to us, we would anathematize him even though he is now dead. But even so, we ought not to abandon, for the sake of any man whatever, the Church of Christ, which is not invented by contentious opinions but proved by divine testimonies.') See, the wonderful preacher both forbids the splitting of the Church for the sake of a man, and does not refuse to anathematize Caecilian, whom he was publicly defending, even after death, should he detect anything perverse in him; because, plainly, the living are truly cared for when a fault committed in the faith is not excused even when death has intervened. But if we should perhaps presume to say that this ought not to be done, we would without doubt be doing what we forbid to be done. For the holy first synod of Ephesus condemned Theodore after his death (Act 6). For when a creed composed by him had been brought before that synod by his disciples, it was at once condemned there by the holy Fathers together with its author. And indeed those holy Fathers who sat in that synod have since been received to the Lord, after they condemned Theodore; and if we say that a dead man ought not to have been condemned, we without doubt accuse the dead, and begin to commit what we strive to forbid. But why do we speak at length of things you know? Let us set out the sayings of this same Theodore from his books. And [see] whether Theodore did not, setting aside all doubt, condemn after death Jesus our Lord and God, who is believed to live after death, or rather because he is believed to live; for our faith does not allow one who stood out as an enemy of our Redeemer with so many blasphemies to be defended by you any longer. For he himself, speaking against Apollinaris in the third book, says (above, collation 4):

X. 'How then do you, to whom above all the governance of minds is most fitting, say that he who was born of the Virgin is God, and is to be thought of as from God, consubstantial with the Father, unless perhaps you do not bid [us] ascribe his creation to the Holy Spirit? But who is God, and from God, and consubstantial with the Father? Is it the same one who had been born of the Virgin (O wonder!), and who was formed through the Holy Spirit according to the divine Scriptures, and received his fashioning in a woman's womb? He was present perhaps, since as soon as he was formed he received [it] that he should be a temple of God; yet we must not think that God was born of the Virgin.' And a little later: 'Nor, according to your saying, is it to be declared that God was at all born of the Virgin, and is from God, consubstantial with the Father.' And a little later: 'If then they say that he was born in the flesh, and that what was born is God and from God and consubstantial with the Father, they must call this too flesh; but if this is not flesh, since it is neither God, nor from God, nor consubstantial with the Father, but of the seed of David and consubstantial with him whose seed it is, then what was born of the Virgin is not God, and from God, and consubstantial with the Father.'

And a little later: 'God the Word was not born of Mary; but he was born of Mary who is of the seed of David; God the Word was not born of a woman.' And again: 'For what is said, He was led by the Spirit (Matt. 4), plainly means this: that he was governed by him, strengthened by him for the will [power] to carry out what was set before him; led by him to the things that were needful, taught by him what was fitting, strengthened by him in his thoughts, so that he might be equal to so great a contest, as blessed Paul also says: For whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God (Rom. 8).'

The same as above: 'Let the wisest of all tell us, then: if, as they say, the Godhead had taken the place of the mind in the Lord Jesus Christ who is according to the flesh, why did Christ need the cooperation of the Holy Spirit for these things? For the Godhead of the Only-begotten did not need the Spirit for justification; [yet] he needed the Spirit to conquer the devil, needed the Spirit to work miracles; needed the Spirit to be taught what it was fitting to accomplish; needed the Spirit to appear spotless.'

And a little later: 'As if Jesus were saying: I, whom you see, can indeed do nothing according to my own nature, since I am a man; but I work, because the Father abiding in me does all things (John 14). For since I too am in the Father, and the Father in me (ibid.), and God the Word, the Only-begotten of God, is in me, it is certain that the Father also abides in me together with him, and does the works. And it is not to be wondered at that these things are thought of Christ, since he himself plainly says of other men: Whoever loves me will keep my word, and the Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him (ibid.).' And again: 'He knew precisely how to make godliness known to the nations, and yet to suffer the infirmities of those who toil, and so to bring his will to effect; and from this he was justified and shown to be spotless, whether by the repair [of worse things], or by the keeping of better things, or also by gradual advances towards better things.'

And a little later, from the commentary of the same Theodore on John: 'He says to Thomas: Bring your finger here and see my hands, and stretch out your hand and put it into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing (John 20). Since, he says, you do not believe, and think that touch alone suffices you for believing (for in saying this you have not escaped my notice), touch with your hand, and take proof, and learn to believe and not to distrust. Thomas, when he had believed in this way, says My Lord and my God, not calling him Lord and God (for the knowledge of the resurrection did not teach that he who rose was also God), but as it were praising God for the miracle that had been done.' From the commentary of the same Theodore on the Acts of the Apostles, book one: 'But he said that they, doing penance for the cross [done] in iniquity, and acknowledging Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord and author of all good things, since through these things he attained and was taken up by the divine nature, ought to receive faith in [him] by the Spirit, and become his disciples, above all coming to baptism, which he himself also handed down to us, having the reformation of the inspiration [the pre-figuring of the hope] of things to come, but to be celebrated in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For this phrase, And let each one be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 2), does not mean that, abandoning the invocation which is in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, one should invoke Jesus Christ in baptism; but just as the phrase that they were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea (1 Cor. 10) means that under the cloud and in the sea they were separated from the Egyptians and freed from their servitude, so as to attend to the laws of Moses; so too is and let each one be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ: that when they had come to him as Saviour and author of all good things and teacher of truth, they should be named after him as author of good things and teacher of truth, just as it is the custom for all men who follow any sect whatever to be named after the very inventor of the doctrine, as Platonists, and Epicureans, and Manichaeans, and Marcionites, and others such are named. For in the same way the apostles judged that we too should be named Christians.'
