From the same Theodore in the books On the Incarnation: 'The Lord was more troubled, and had a greater contest, with the passions of the soul than with those of the body; and he overcame the desires with a better mind, the Godhead mediating towards perfection. Hence the Lord seems to have undertaken the contest chiefly against these.'

Likewise from the same, in the book against the Synousiasts, or Apollinarists: 'But if it was flesh, he says, that was crucified, how did the sun turn away its rays, and darkness cover the whole earth, and the earth quake, and the rocks split, and the dead rise (Matt. 27)? What then would they say of the darkness that came over Egypt in the time of Moses, not for three hours but for three days (Exod. 10)? And what of the other miracles done through Moses, and those through Joshua son of Nun, who made the sun stand still (Josh. 10), of the sun which in the time of King Hezekiah was turned back even against nature (4 Kings 20), and of the bones of Elisha, which raised a dead man (4 Kings 13)?' From the same, from the eighth book On the Incarnation: 'It is clear that unity is fitting; for through it the natures brought together have produced one person according to the unity. For just as it is said of a man and a woman that they are no longer two but one flesh (Gen. 2; Matt. 19), let us also say reasonably, according to the principle of unity, that they are not two persons but one, the natures, that is, being distinct.'

And a little later: 'How then can man and God be one through unity? He who gives life and he who is given life; he who saves and he who is saved; he who is before the ages and he who appeared from Mary?' From the same, from the interpretation of the creed of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers: 'But [he speaks] of Christ according to the form of a servant that was assumed, while naming him who assumed it God over all; yet he added this according to the conjunction, so as to make a clear division through the meaning of the names of the natures. Let no one, then, call him who is from the Jews according to the flesh God, nor again [call] God [another reading: Lord] who is over all, from the Jews according to the flesh.'

Likewise from the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews: 'For he speaks of Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10); but he who was anointed by the Spirit certainly took something from it. And who but a madman would say that the divine nature took something from the Spirit?' And again: 'He himself was certain [of it], calling himself Son of God not according to the birth of the Godhead, but in that he was of God's household; by which men made members of God's household through good will [power] were meanwhile called sons of God.'

XI. These few things out of countless ones we have brought forward, so as to show, as it were through a narrow opening, what an enormous abyss lay hidden within. See of what sort are the more than ten thousand books Theodore is said to have written. Consider, I beg you, whether he has not deserved torments all the sharper the more he wrote. But perhaps it is doubted whether these sayings of his that have been brought forward are really his. Let us, if you please, bring forward the writings of the Fathers: thus, by bringing in further witnesses, let us confirm to you his books, which we have brought in as witnesses of his faithlessness. For the bishops of Armenia, presenting petitions against Theodore to Proclus, bishop of the city of Constantinople, say (above, collation 5): 'There was a certain pestilent man, or rather a beast with a diabolical human form, Theodore by a false name, who held the guise and name of bishop, lurking in an obscure and ignoble corner of the world, in the town of Mopsuestia in Cilicia Secunda, truly and chiefly descended from Paul of Samosata, though in his book on the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ he is found throughout his whole purpose to have used the very words of Photinus and the other heresiarchs, and anything worse there is. This man, by the contrivance, audacity and error of the devil, wished all men to perish by his sharp tongue, like a snake's, and by the poison which is under the tongue of the asp. And for a time indeed he kept to his lair, fearing the power of those who received power from our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ to tread upon snakes and scorpions and all the forces of the enemy (Luke 10): I mean the holy apostles, and those who received [it] from them in succession, martyrs and confessors and bishops and the other saints. But having found an opportunity, I know not how, he began to creep out even beyond his own bounds, growing bold, and in a parish not belonging to him, as a learned speaker, addressing the church at Antioch in Syria, he spoke thus: "The man Jesus — for what is man that you are mindful of him? (Ps. 8); and the Apostle said this was said of Jesus: For we see him who was made a little lower than the angels, he says, Jesus (Heb. 2). What then? The man Jesus is like all men, having no difference from men of the same kind except what grace gave him."' Replying to them, Proclus, bishop of the city of Constantinople, says (above, collation 5, council 5): 'Let us flee the turbid and muddy streams of deceit, the enclosures [sects] that fight against God: I mean the fury of Arius, dividing the indivisible Trinity; the audacity of Eunomius, enclosing in knowledge the incomprehensible nature; the rage of Macedonius, separating from the Godhead the Spirit who proceeds inseparably; and those introducing this new blasphemy, which far surpasses the blasphemy of Judaism; for they, when they deny the Son, rob the root of its branch; but these, denying him who is, introduce another [another reading: deny him who is the Son, robbing the root of its branch, but these introduce another besides him who is], disparaging the pure nature.' (Again, concerning his error, John, bishop of the Church of Antioch, also says: 'Theodore, persisting for a long time, persuaded many, and Nestorius, that Christ the Son of the living God, who was born of the holy Virgin Mary, is not God the Word born of the Father, consubstantial with the Begetter, but a man receiving cooperation from God the Word according to the quality of his own will.') Again, concerning his error, Cyril, writing to the presbyter Lampon, says: 'When I was staying at Aelia, a man, one of those who serve nobly in the palace, presented to me a long, sealed letter of many lines, which he said he had received from the orthodox of Antioch; and there were in it the signatures of very many clerics, monks and laymen. They accused the eastern bishops of keeping silent, as it were, about the name of Nestorius and pretending to oppose him, while going over to the books of Theodore written on the Incarnation, in which far worse impious blasphemies [than those of Nestorius] are set down; for he was the father of the faithless Nestorius, who, having spoken his evils, also became impious in these things.' Again, concerning his error, the same Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, writing to Acacius, bishop of the city of Melitene, says: 'It ought not to have escaped your Holiness, or perhaps you have learned, that all the most religious eastern bishops met at Antioch, when my lord the most holy Proclus had sent them a tome full of good understandings and right doctrines. For there was in it a long and extended discourse on the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ. And he appended certain chapters collected from the books of Theodore, which have an understanding consonant with the faithless doctrines of Nestorius, and urged them to anathematize these too.'

XII. Again, concerning his error, [Rabbula], bishop of the church of Edessa, writing to the blessed Cyril, says: 'But now certain people reject in every way the unity according to subsistence. For a disease lying hidden has grown old in the East, feeding on the body of the Church like an incurable wound, secretly honoured among some who are, as it were, studious and who raise their eyebrows over their learning. For a certain Theodore, bishop of the province of Cilicia, a man plausible in speech and powerful in persuasion, said some things from the tribunal about the state of the Church [another reading: in church immediately] to please the people, but laid other snares [of perdition] in his writings; at the beginning of certain of his books he bound the reader by anathema not to reveal the writings to others. He was the first to set out that the holy Virgin is not truly the Mother of God, as though God the Word had not undergone birth as we do. (And a little later:) For they do not say that the man was united to God the Word according to substance or according to subsistence, but by a certain good will, as though the divine nature could not admit another mode of unity because it cannot be circumscribed. He said that our Lord Jesus Christ ought not to be adored as Lord, but honoured by reference to God as a kind of image; or rather, to put it more plainly according to them, like something by reference to an attendant demon. He also declared that the flesh of the Lord profits nothing at all, twisting the Lord's saying, which is: The flesh profits nothing (John 6). He also says that the apostles did not know that Christ was God, but that the Church was built upon faith in a man (Matthew 16).'

XIII. Again, concerning his error, Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem, a writer of ecclesiastical history, says: 'Thus a certain Theodore particularly imitated Photinus, who lived many ages before them; he was malicious in speech and very ready of tongue, yet himself of unstable will, carried this way and that as he leaned. For, enrolled from his early youth among the clergy of Antioch and having promised to live well, he turned back and again took delight in worldly lusts. But John, bishop of Constantinople, a blessed man worthy of imitation in all good things, wrote a letter, which is read in the books to this day, and prevailed to bring him from the worse to a better repentance; and he began again to live well and again to be in the clergy. And leaving Antioch he moved to Tarsus, and from there he passed to Mopsuestia, where he was ordained bishop, since God did not yet will that the preaching of his impiety should become manifest. Beginning the first elements of his doctrine from Jewish idle talk, he wrote a book on the prophecy of the Psalms which denied all the preachings [perhaps: predictions] about the Lord; but when blamed and endangered, he said things contrary to himself, not of his own will but compelled by everyone's complaints; and having promised to destroy the book itself, he secretly kept it as provision for Jewish impiety.' And a little later: 'For Christ Jesus, the Saviour and Lord of our race (whom Paul calls the radiance of the Father's glory and the image of his substance [Hebrews 1], saying that he upholds all things by the word of his power, who made purification for our sins and sat down at the right hand of the Father's majesty; of whom he wrote in the epistle to the Colossians: That in him all things were created that are in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, that all things were created through him [Colossians 1]) — this one, the man foolish in all things wrote, was not the Word incarnate, as we have been taught by the words of the Gospel, but a man joined to God the Word through progress of life and perfection of sufferings. And this he dared [to say] in mystical discourses.'

XIV. Against the errors of the same Theodore, Theodosius and Valentinian of pious memory, promulgating a law, say: 'Rendering to the most pious doctrine the veneration we owe it, we have judged that those who have dared to write impiously against God ought to be subjected to due condemnation and called by fitting names. It is just, then, that they be surrounded with the shame of their sins and remain under such a name for ever, so that they may neither be freed while living nor, after death, cease to be held in contempt. Therefore the doctrine of the impious and pestilent Theodore and Nestorius has seemed to us abominable; and likewise it is just that all who follow their error and consent to their impiety should deserve the same name and be clothed with shame, so that they be called not Christians but Nestorians; lest, while called Christians, they be found adorned with that very name though placed far from the purpose of Christians and estranged from the right and spotless faith.' And a little later: 'If anyone transgresses our present sanction, so as to assent to Theodore and Nestorius and imitate their associates, after the punishment of the sword let all his property be confiscated to the treasury.' (Again against his errors Theodosius and Valentinian of pious memory, promulgating a law, say: 'Let no one have, read, copy or bring forward Nestorius or his books, or the wholly useless [harmful] books, whether of Nestorius himself or of another, and especially those written by Nestorius against Christians alone, or of Theodore; but let each one who has such books bring them out publicly and commit them to the fire in the sight of all.')

XV. And if perhaps, after so many judgements of the Fathers brought forward against him, your Fraternity still doubts, let it read the books of Theodoret, in which, while he strives to defend him against Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, he rather accuses him, saying: 'Cyril accuses the interpretation of the eighth psalm, and censures these words of the divine Theodore: Let us consider, then, who is the man at whom he is astonished and marvels that the Only-begotten deigned to be mindful of him and to visit him. But that this was not said of every man has been shown above; and that [another reading: nor] [it was said] of any one man at random, this too is certain.' Who, then, doubts that these blasphemies, established by so many witnesses, are his? And with so many of his blasphemies known, who would deny that he was rightly condemned?

XVI. Having therefore discussed the first chapter, on the condemnation of Theodore, let us now pass to examining the words of the letter of Theodoret [Ibas], whose whole tenor, if carefully examined, is judged to be how opposed to the holy synod of Chalcedon. For in the acts of that synod and in the writings of Leo, Cyril is praised; but in that letter of Theodoret, Cyril is rejected as falling into the doctrine of Apollinaris; for it is written in it: 'But Cyril, wishing to destroy the books of Nestorius, slipped and was found falling into the doctrine of Apollinaris.' In the acts, Nestorius is shown to have been rightly condemned as an adversary of our Redeemer; but in the words of the letter he is said to have been condemned unjustly. For thus it says in it: 'Before the most reverend and most holy archbishop John arrived at the synod, they deposed Nestorius from the episcopate, without a trial or inquiry being made.' In the acts of the synod Cyril is shown to have confessed two natures in the one person of our God and Lord; in the words of the letter he is said to teach one nature, and, rebuked from this view, is related to have barely come to his senses. In the acts of the synod Nestorius is said to have been anathematized even after death; but in the words of the letter he is reported, even after his deposition, not to have returned to his city solely because of the hatred of his citizens. For thus it is written there: 'But Nestorius, because he was hated by his city and by the greatest men in it, could not return there.' In the acts and definitions of the synod one Son, Jesus Christ, is spoken of; but according to the doctrine of Theodore and Nestorius, God is passed over in silence. And in the acts of the synod Theodore is nowhere called a teacher of truth; but in the words of the letter the same man, whose blasphemies we have set out above, is proclaimed a teacher of truth: and certainly, if he spoke truly, what the synod set forth about the truth will be false. Whoever, then, strives to show that the letter said to be of Ibas belongs to the synod, what else does he attempt but to destroy the acts of that same synod? For if they are at variance with themselves, they will without doubt stand on no authority, since things that destroy themselves by attacking each other cannot build up others; if they are at variance with themselves, they gain no firmness, as the Lord testifies, who says: A kingdom divided against itself will not stand (Luke 11). But far be this, far be it from that venerable council, that it should hold views contrary to itself, and either set earlier things in discord before later ones, or append later things to attack earlier ones. For the holy faith, which was received there with one spirit, was believed with one mind, and was preached with one faith [perhaps: voice]. For this reason it has become the pattern of our profession in all parts of the world, because in the voices of those who pray it is not unlike itself.

XVII. But why do we say only that the holy synod of Chalcedon is overthrown if we do not deny authority to this letter? For indeed, if it is believed true, the whole faith and reverence of the holy synod of Ephesus too is destroyed. For it says that in it Cyril blinded the eyes of the wise with the drug of rewards. What, then, is said there with certainty about the truth, where truth itself is reported to have been sold to the bishops? But who would say this, who would consent to hear this patiently? Let the one lying letter, then, be rejected, lest both holy synods bear the charge of so great a falsehood. We hold the foundation of your faith, lest, after the holy first synod of Ephesus is accused as if venal, that of Chalcedon too (which God forbid) be branded with the fault of inconsistency; and so that it may be clear how great is the concord in its words, it is necessary that your Fraternity know where it was completed. For we all know that in a synod canons are never held except when the definitions of faith have been carried through and the synodal acts completed, so that, the order being kept, when the synod has first built up hearts in the faith, it then orders the morals and actions of the Church by the rules of the canons. Consider, therefore, with watchful care that in its sixth session the profession of the holy faith is completed; and immediately in the seventh the rule of the canons is fixed for the instruction of those now faithful. In the later sessions, however, nothing is dealt with concerning the cause of faith, but only private business. Since your envoys were in doubt about this, we took care to demonstrate it from many books brought forward. We, however, believed that this could never be doubted, since the very sequence presents itself in such a way that it contradicts believing otherwise.

XVIII. First, because (as has been said) while the defined rule of faith is shown in the sixth session, the order of the proceedings indicates that in the session joined to it the form of the canons should follow. Second, because already at the end of the sixth session the norm of the canons is touched on in advance, when the emperor there says to the venerable bishops: There are some chapters which, for the honour of your Reverence, we have reserved to you, thinking it right that these be confirmed by you canonically, point by point, through the synod, etc. By this foretaste in the sixth session, then, it is shown that the enactments of the canons are rightly contained only in the seventh. For what remained to be done, once the profession of faith was completed, except that the holy synod, having laid down rules, should judge the unlawful actions of certain of the faithful? And yet, if we look carefully, we find that the rules of the canons were laid down not, as is supposed, in the seventh session, but woven into the sixth. For since in the enactment of these same constitutions no date is set down, no reign, and those who presided are not described, it is beyond doubt shown, since they did not begin with the customary opening, that they are attached to the preceding session. That the cause of faith is completed in the sixth session is declared by the general subscription of all the bishops itself. For those who subscribed to the judgement thereby testified that everything that was to be done concerning the faith was finished. Hence also in the later particular cases they speak only in bare words, and confirmed what they had said in their decisions with no subscription added. And the most reverend bishops recognised that everything that was to be done concerning the faith was [finished] in the sixth session, so that, as is written there, they cried out: We beg you, release us, pious emperor, release us. (And that they were detained not for the faith but for particular cases is shown there by the emperor's reply, when it is said: Our most sacred and most pious lord Marcian Augustus said to the holy synod: You have laboured a long time and endured weariness; but bear with it three or four days more, and in the presence of our most magnificent judges raise each matter you wish, and you will obtain fitting relief [another reading: help].) Since, then, they were retained to raise whatever particular matters they wished, it is clear that they by no means remained beyond the end of the sixth session for the cause of faith.

But why do we treat these things at length, we who are supported by such great authority of our predecessor the blessed Leo? For he, as we have shown above by the testimony of many of his letters, by disapproving the manifold acts concerning particular cases, restricted the authority of the synod to the definition of faith alone. Hence it is that, after the synod was over, wiping away for us all clouds of suspicion, he writes openly to Maximus, bishop of the see of Antioch, saying (Letter 62): If anything is said to have been done by those brothers whom I sent to the holy synod in my place, beyond what pertained to the cause of faith, it will be of no validity at all, because they were sent by the apostolic see only for this, that, heresies being cut away, they should be defenders of the catholic faith. For whatever, apart from the particular causes of synodal councils, is brought to episcopal examination can have some ground for being judged afresh. (But some are accustomed to say that he said this on account of the presumption of Anatolius, bishop of the city of Constantinople; but if they consider both the events and the words of the letters we have now brought forward, they at once cease to suspect falsely. For when the aforesaid bishop of the city of Constantinople was attempting to seize something new, it is established that the legates of the apostolic see resisted him there with the utmost freedom of authority (Session 16). This is both read as done in the synod, and is confirmed by the letters of that same synod to our aforesaid predecessor. And we know that our same oft-mentioned predecessor wrote to Maximus, as we said before: If anything is said to have been done by those brothers whom I sent to the holy synod in my place, beyond what pertained to the cause of faith, it will be of no validity at all, because they were sent by the apostolic see only for this, that, heresies being cut away, they should be defenders of the catholic faith. If, then, speaking of the case of Anatolius, he refuted what had been done by his vicars in the synod, he was surely rebuking them for having objected. And who, even a fool, would think this? Since it is established that on this matter the blessed Leo, replying to Anatolius when he complained, writes much in praise of his vicars because they had objected (Letter 53); the words of that letter we do not set down now, so as not to extend this volume beyond measure.) When it is further added: For whatever, apart from the particular causes of synodal councils, is brought to episcopal examination can have some ground for being judged afresh, (licence is openly granted to us to reconsider whatever was done there concerning persons outside the causes of faith. For the particular cause of synodal councils is the faith. Whatever, therefore, is done apart from the faith, as Leo teaches, is shown to be such that nothing prevents it from being recalled to judgement. And that among those same bishops who sat at Chalcedon the synod was held in veneration only as far as the definition of faith is openly shown by this: that many older Greek manuscripts are shown to contain the synod only in six sessions, with the canons attached, so that they do not have at all the other things that had been raised from private interest. Hence the Encyclia too testify that this is so. For Alypius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, writing to the emperor Leo, says (In part 3 of the Council of Chalcedon, ch. 50): These things being so, I inform your Piety that I have not read the matters examined individually and the things done by the holy bishops gathered in the city of Chalcedon; for nothing more of what is known to have been done was brought here by Thalassius, of holy memory, then bishop, who took part in the holy council, but I examined only the definition set forth by that holy council, which he brought.) By the testimony of bishop Alypius, then, we are taught that Thalassius held nothing of the synod in veneration beyond the cause of faith, although he took part there also, beyond the cause of faith, in the private business of the bishops. If, then, the profession of faith is completed in the sixth session, and immediately the rule of the canons is fixed; if the blessed Leo opposes the business privately raised there; if what was done beyond the faith was not upheld even by Thalassius, who did it: why are we blamed for having reconsidered a heretical letter, we who in this matter are strengthened by the authority of all who went before us? And although Ibas answers that the letter is foreign to him; although it can be shown only with difficulty, or not at all, that it was approved, yet anyone might freely censure it even if the bishops sitting in that council had approved it with their subscriptions; because once, by the writing of the blessed Leo, the right to reconsider and judge afresh is granted, whatever authority those who took part might have had in private business is made void.

XX. The second chapter having thus been examined, the third remains, which we ought to compress the more briefly as we do not believe that you oppose us in this matter. For we do not condemn all the writings of Theodoret, but only those which he is shown to have written at some time against the twelve chapters of Cyril, only those against the right faith; which he himself is known to have condemned, since in the holy synod of Chalcedon he is found to have confessed the truth. For how, after error, he came to think rightly is made plain both by what he had written before and by what he did at the synod of Chalcedon. For writing to Nestorius he says (Collation 3): 'To the things unjustly and wickedly pronounced against your Veneration, I shall not be able to give consent, not even if someone cuts off both my hands.' Writing also to Aemerius [another reading: Himerius], bishop of Nicomedia, he says (Synodal letter 71): 'We ought not to give consent to the condemnation, said to be being made, of the venerable and most holy bishop Nestorius.' (Writing also to Alexander, bishop of Hierapolis, he says: 'I told your Holiness before that, if the teaching of my lord the venerable and most holy bishop Nestorius should be condemned, I would not communicate with those who do it.') And writing to Alexander, bishop of Syria of the Palestinians, he says: 'I think that above all my lord the most holy and venerable bishop John has been fully satisfied that I will in no way agree to give consent to the condemnation of my lord the most holy and venerable bishop Nestorius, which was made at Tarsus and at Ephesus.' (Yet afterwards, when he was admitted by the holy council of Chalcedon amid the struggle of those opposing, he openly pronounced anathema on Nestorius, and showed himself orthodox by rejecting that heretic. For formerly, thinking otherwise than the holy Church, and writing against the twelve chapters of the blessed Cyril, he says (In part 5 of the Council of Ephesus, on the 5th anathema): 'We call the holy Virgin theotokos, that is, Mother of God, not because she bore God by nature, but because she brought forth a man joined to God, whom he himself formed.') And a little after: 'If a natural union was made of the form of God and the form of a servant, the lawgiver will be found serving the necessities of the law.' (And again [on the 5th anathema]: 'Relying on the term communion, we adore as one Son both him who assumed and him who was assumed; yet we recognise the difference of the natures. And we do not refuse to call the man Christ theophoros, that is, God-bearing, or one who has put on the Lord, as has indeed been said by many of the Fathers.' And after other things [on the 10th anathema]: 'Consider,' he says, 'the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, faithful to him who made him (Hebr. 3), as Moses also was in all his house. But who, thinking rightly, would say that he who is uncreated and co-eternal with the Father, and I will add, true [God the Word], is something made? Rather [it is] he who is of the seed of David, who, free from all sin, was our high priest, and himself offered himself for us as a victim to God, having in himself certainly the Word of God united to him and inseparably joined.') And again, as if to show that he grew into divinity by increments, he adds in the same work, saying: 'The angel says to the Virgin: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you: and therefore the holy one who will be born of you will be called the Son of God (Luke 1). Consider here too that all things are said in a human way: He will be, it says, great; it did not say, is; and he will be called son of the Most High; it did not say, is called; and the Lord will give him the throne of David his father; it did not say, has, but the Lord will give him; and he will reign; it did not say, reigns; and over whom? over the house of Jacob; it did not say, over angels and archangels.') Again in the same second book he says: 'And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan (Luke 4:1). And again: Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee (ibid. 14): do not think that God the Word needed the cooperation or help of the Holy Spirit, but the visible temple enjoyed the various gifts of the Holy Spirit.' (And after other things: 'Jesus Christ,' he says, 'yesterday and today, the same also for ever. How then, most wise ones, must we take note how the same one is yesterday and today and for ever, both temporal and eternal, both in time and above times: for if he is eternal, he is not temporal, and if he is in time, he is not above time.' And again, asserting as it were a unity of deity and humanity in our Lord God Jesus Christ, he says: 'We distinguish the natures of God the Word; we call it a whole nature, and a person without doubt perfect; for it is not right to assert a substance without a person; we likewise confess the human nature perfect with its own person. But when we look to the union, then at last we rightly name one person.') Who, dearest brothers, does not see that these things are full of all impiety? Yet it is established that he afterwards corrected himself from them, since in the holy synod of Chalcedon he agreed to anathematise Nestorius. Who does not see how full of rashness it is proudly to defend the writings of Theodoret which it is established that he himself condemned, professing rightly afterwards? We accept him and his person, and we reject the wicked writings which had formerly lain hidden, and in nothing do we depart from the proceedings of the holy synod: because, rejecting only his heretical writings, we still pursue Nestorius together with the synod, and together with the synod we venerate Theodoret professing aright (above, Collation 4). His other writings we not only accept, but we even use them against opponents. For when Theodore wished to expound the Song of Songs, and laboured not at commentary but rather at ravings, he declared that by this book [Solomon] had flattered the Ethiopian queen; and Theodoret, censuring this, suppresses indeed the name of that Theodore, but nevertheless laid bare his madness. For writing a commentary on that same book, he says (in the preface): I hear that many disparage the Song of Songs and do not believe it to be a spiritual book, but, weaving certain old wives' tales in their madness, compose and presume, saying that the wise Solomon wrote this book about himself and the daughter of Pharaoh. How then do we accept none of the writings of this same Theodoret, when we find him to be an upholder of the truth even against Theodore? This is our reply to your writings.

XXI. But we judge it very fitting to go over briefly the words which we heard from your envoys without writing. For they said that Theodore was praised with remarkable testimony by John, bishop of the city of Antioch, in a letter; which we in no way believe to be true. If, however, something of the kind is perhaps found, we give more credence to the first synod of Ephesus, more to the books of Cyril, more to those of Hesychius, than to other letters which up to now have not been able to become known. We ought, however, to go further, even granting something [for the sake of] argument. Let us suppose, then, that it is as your envoys assert. You know, dearest brothers, that a matter which lies open to doubt is always to be interpreted in the better sense. What, then, stands in the way, if, while his error was still hidden and doubtful, he was praised by one Father; and afterwards, when his treachery became known, he was pierced by the judgements of almost all the great Fathers, as a monstrous beast is by ever thickening darts? Or do we not know that bad men have sometimes been praised by good men, and yet not defended by those same praises? For what can be found more deplorable among heresiarchs than Origen, and what more honourable among historians than Eusebius? And which of us does not know with how many commendations Eusebius extols Origen in his books? But because the holy Church weighs the hearts of her faithful more kindly than their words strictly, neither could the testimony of Eusebius absolve the heretic's own meaning, nor in turn did the guilt of the Origen he had praised condemn Eusebius. Does not Gregory too, bishop of the city of Nyssa, when he expounds the Song of Songs, set Origen forward with great praises? Is not Jerome too, presbyter of our Church and singular interpreter of the Hebrew tongue, so eager in his favour towards Origen that he almost seems to be his disciple? But because the case is to be weighed more than the words, neither did his own kindness harm the one, nor did the favour of another's testimony excuse the other from his own guilt.

XXII. After this, dearest brothers, I am compelled to say in sorrow with Paul: I bear you witness that you have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. 10); and when I look upon his heart of charity towards the unity of the holy Church, I lament all the more unbearably that you are in discord. Consider, I beg, with what ardour he longed for holy unity when he said to the Philippians: If there is any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of charity, if any hope of fellowship, if any heart and mercies, fulfil my joy, that you be of the same mind, having the same charity, of one accord, thinking the same thing (Phil. 2). He, then, who was about to speak of unanimity and set before it so many and such questions, showed how great the merit of this virtue is not by fully stating it but by asking. But on the other hand, speaking to the Corinthians, he shows how evil discord is. For he says: It has been made known to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who are of Chloe's household, that there are contentions among you; I mean this, that each of you says, I am of Paul, and I of Apollo, and I of Cephas, and I of Christ (1 Cor. 3). With how much severity he says this we recognise if we weigh the words of the rebuke that follows. For he says: Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptised in the name of Paul? (ibid.). Consider, then, my brothers, and while God still waits and we are left with the end of life wholly uncertain, weigh with watchful care that your Fraternity is not afraid to make for Theodore that schism of the holy Church which Paul shrank even from declaring for his own sake. Why is the saying of the blessed Augustine about preserving unity not called to mind (Augustine, book On the One Baptism)? He, speaking of the one baptism, declared that the martyr Cyprian, who had written on repeating baptism, died [in the Church] for this reason: that although he held a somewhat erroneous view, he nevertheless never cut himself off from the communion of the whole Church. It is clear, then, dearest brothers, [what it is] to remain in holiness while preserving [unity]: because, while you sever yourselves from the unity of the Church, you have lost all the merit of virtue, even if you hold rightly. For it is written: Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord (Heb. 12).

XXIII. We have said much, because we have also answered many points by reasoning. And though countless testimonies from the sayings of the Fathers were at hand, we have set down very few, wishing, that is, that a shortened account should keep our writing concise on each matter, lest perhaps it breed weariness in the reader. One thing, however, which we have already said above, we are not wearied to repeat even often: that by God's authority we keep the faith of the holy synod of Chalcedon unimpaired in all things, and its definitions, like those of the first synod of Ephesus, of Constantinople, and of Nicaea, we have held up to now as not to be retracted, and we guard them as not to be retracted even with death set before us. Let your Affection, then, not flee the communion of faithful orthodox brothers, lest, if it neglects to hear the help of our present voice, it turn it into a testimony against itself. As for us, after words we have recourse to the Lord, and we entreat him with tears as much as we can, that what we say to you for following concord he himself may work in your minds by the hand of inward inspiration.
LETTER VI (formerly VIII),
TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.
He rebukes him for claiming for himself the name of universal bishop, on which ground he had convoked a general synod.
To the most beloved brothers, all the bishops who, at the unlawful summons of John, bishop of Constantinople, came together at Constantinople for a synod, Pelagius.

Since (as we desired) through the grace of God the night of most pernicious error has been driven from the universal Church by the light of gospel truth, we rejoice inexpressibly in the Lord; but we are saddened with no small grief, because things which were once trodden down and utterly condemned, and ought never to have been done, are sprouting and springing up from revived roots. And since many things are happening which can produce repentance, it is necessary to annul those which are known to have been done against order and all authority. Therefore, brothers, let the audacity be wholly cast off which has been taken up to dispute against the commands of the Lord, against the apostolic see and against the very voice of the Lord Saviour, by which it was said: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church (Matt. 16); let the vain hearts of those who err be quiet, and let it not be lawful to defend what it is not lawful to do. It has been reported, then, to the apostolic see that John, bishop of Constantinople, signs himself universal, and that on this presumption of his he has summoned you to a general synod, although the authority of convoking general synods has been entrusted to the apostolic see of blessed Peter by a singular privilege, and no synod is ever read of as valid which was not supported by apostolic authority. Wherefore, whatever you have decreed in the aforesaid conventicle (since a synod presumed in such a way could not be a synod), by the authority of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and by the voice of the Lord Saviour, by which the Saviour himself gave blessed Peter the power of binding and loosing, which power has also undoubtedly passed to his successors, I command that all that you decreed there be void and annulled, so that henceforth it may never appear nor be discussed. For the Saviour himself, as truth itself speaking in its own person, says to the blessed apostle Peter: Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven (Matt. 16). Again we are instructed by many apostolic, canonical and ecclesiastical rules that councils ought not to be held without the judgement of the Roman pontiff; wherefore (as has already been said) not a council but your conventicle or petty council is rightly annulled, and whatever was done in it is held null and void. You too [are to take care] henceforth not to presume such things at anyone's urging, if you do not wish to lack the communion of the apostolic see. For now, however, punishment is suspended so that correction may have room. Indeed John's predecessors, and John himself, not once but very often sent to our holy predecessors letters and petitions signed with their own hand, in which they declared before God that they would never do anything insolently against the apostolic see, nor usurp anything of its privileges or those of others; and these are kept intact up to now in the archive of the holy Roman Church, confirmed under their seals and signatures. For in these very letters or petitions they bound themselves and their successors with the bond of anathema, if they should ever presume anything against them, or in any way contrive anything hostile against the apostolic see or the see of any other bishop. Therefore it is not necessary to excommunicate or anathematise them, because they have bound themselves with the bond of anathema by confirming their professions and their writings with their own hands. Let John himself know, however, that unless he quickly corrects his error, he will be excommunicated by us and will lack the communion of the apostolic see and of all holy bishops. Pay no heed either to the name of universality which he has unlawfully usurped for himself, and never come at his summons to a synod without the authority of the apostolic see, if you wish to enjoy the communion of the apostolic see and of the other bishops. For let none of the patriarchs ever use this so profane a title, because if the highest [another reading: one] patriarch is called universal, the name of patriarch is taken from the rest. But far be it from the mind of any faithful man that anyone should wish to seize for himself something by which he might seem to diminish the honour of his brothers in even the smallest part. Wherefore let your Charity never name anyone universal in your letters, lest you withdraw from yourselves what is due when you offer another an undue honour. For our adversary the devil, who, raging against the humble, goes about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5), now, as we see, does not merely go round the sheepfolds, but fixes his tooth strongly in certain necessary members of the Church; so that no one may doubt that, unless the provident company of all the shepherds runs together with one mind, with the Lord's favour, he will soon tear apart the whole fold, which God forbid. Consider, dearest brothers, what follows close at hand, when such perverse beginnings break out even among priests. For he is near of whom it is written: He is king over all the sons of pride (Job 41) (which I am compelled to say not without heavy grief, since our brother and fellow bishop John, despising the Lord's commands, the apostolic precepts and the rules of the Fathers, tries through pride to run ahead of him in name). May almighty God show your Beatitude with what heavy groaning at this thought I am tormented: that he who was once well known to me, he who was loved by all, he who seemed occupied with almsgiving, prayers and fasts, has taken such boastfulness from the ashes on which he sat and from the humility which he displayed, that he tries to ascribe everything to himself, and strives through the choice of a pompous word to subject to himself all the members which cleave to the one head alone, namely Christ, the members of that same Christ. Nor is it surprising that that tempter, who knows that pride is the beginning of all sin, and who then used it before all else in the first man, now sets it in certain men at the end of their virtues; and for those who by good pursuits of life seemed in some measure to escape his most cruel hands, he sets a snare at the very goal of good work and, as it were, at the very conclusion of perfection. Hence we must pray earnestly, and implore almighty God with constant prayers, that he turn this error from that man's mind and remove this evil of pride and confusion from the unity and humility of the Church; and, with God's favour, we must run together and take care with all our strength, lest by the poison of one word living members in the body of Christ should die. For if this is freely permitted to be said, the honour of all the patriarchs is denied; and perhaps he who is called universal perishes in error, and then no bishop is found to have remained in the state of truth. You must therefore keep the churches as you received them, firmly and without prejudice, and let this temptation of diabolical usurpation claim nothing for itself in you. Stand firm, stand secure; never presume either to give or to accept writings condemned by the falsehood of the universal name. Keep all the bishops subject to your care from the defilement of this flattery, so that the whole Church may recognise you as patriarchs not only in good works but also in the authority of truth. And if perhaps some adversities follow, persisting with one mind we ought to show, even by dying, that we do not love anything of our own in particular to the detriment of the whole. Let us say with Paul: For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil. 1). Let us hear what the first of all the apostles says: If you suffer anything for justice' sake, you will be blessed (1 Pet. 3). For believe me, the honour which we received for preaching the truth we relinquish, if the cause of necessity demands, more securely for that same truth than we hold it. [Up to this point the words of Saint Gregory, interpolated or corrupted.] Pray, brothers, that ecclesiastical honour be not emptied in our days, and that the Roman see, which (by the Lord's institution) is the head of all Churches, may never anywhere lack or be stripped of its privileges. But we are confident of better things concerning you, dearest ones, and things nearer to salvation: because neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature (as the Teacher of the Gentiles teaches) will be able to separate us from the charity of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the right faith which is in him. Do not, therefore, cast away your confidence, which has a great reward (Heb. 5, Rom. 8, Heb. 10).

For patience is necessary for us against the struggles of the adversaries, so that, keeping the faith unblemished to the end, we may receive the promise which he has promised to those who hasten to contend lawfully. For yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come, and will not delay (Hab. 2, according to the LXX). For behold, the judge stands before the door (Jas. 5), joyfully promising crowns to those who submit to sufferings for him. But if anyone withdraws, he will not please my soul, and he will fall from the promise because of his denial. But we are not sons of withdrawal unto the perdition of the soul. Therefore take up the armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day against all the enemies of the holy Church of God and your own; and put on the breastplate of justice, having your feet shod in preparation of the gospel of peace, in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to quench all the fiery darts of the most wicked one; and receive the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God, through all prayer and supplication, rooted and grounded in the support of the brothers, for Christ Jesus our Lord (Heb. 10; Eph. 6).

But now also, brothers, we commend you all to the Lord and to the word of his grace, who is able to accomplish [all] and to give you an inheritance with all the saints. May the God of peace and consolation himself grant you to be of the same mind towards one another, so that you may help one another and not be divided, so that with one mind, with one mouth and one heart, we may honour him, in concord and consolation of the brothers, who is able to strengthen you according to his gospel, and according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages

(Acts 20; Rom. 15, 16), by which the gifts of future joys are to be bestowed on you. You ought also to consider above all that those who envy their brothers and desire to condemn or destroy them destroy themselves and their own teachings by their own act. For the Lord says: Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand; and every knowledge and law divided against itself will not stand (Matt. 12). Therefore it is necessary that you receive salutary exhortations in concord [St Leo, letter 87], and, doing nothing out of contention, but united in all zeal of devotion, obey the divine and apostolic constitutions, and in nothing allow the most provident decrees of the canons to be violated, so that both the constitutions of the Nicene canons and what has been providently and salutarily decreed by us or by our predecessors may remain unblemished in the future. And in the Apocalypse the Lord speaks through John, saying: Do not fear, I am the first and the last, and the living one; and I was dead, and behold, I am living for ever and ever (Apoc. 1). And: I have the keys of death and of hell. And a little later: To him who conquers I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God (Apoc. 2). And the same [Rom. ed.: likewise]: Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. And again: He who conquers and keeps my works to the end, I will give him power over the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron, and like a potter's vessel they will be broken. Likewise the same: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with me. He who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne (Apoc. 3). You, brothers, if you do not wish to be condemned with him (for not only those who do [such things], but those who consent to those who do them, are guilty (Rom. 1)), exhort him and warn him to withdraw from the aforesaid unlawful things, and let him remember whence he has fallen, and do penance, and do the first works. Otherwise, I will speak not my own words but those of the Lord the Saviour himself, which he spoke through the aforesaid John in the book already mentioned; repeating them, I say: I will come and will move your lampstand from its place, unless you do penance (Apoc. 2). For he rather holds the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to cast a stumbling-block before the sons of Israel, just as this man teaches you to scandalize holy mother Church and the whole body both of priests and of religious Christians and faithful. Hence in the above-mentioned book it is also contained thus (for I always desire to strike and instruct you with the words of the Lord the Saviour rather than with my own, although these too are full of the weight of apostolic authority): I know your works, the last more than the first. But I have a few things against you [Rom. ed. lacks 'a few'], because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols. And I gave her time to do penance, and she does not wish to repent of her fornication. Behold, I cast her into a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into very great tribulation, unless they do penance for their works; and I will kill her children with death. And all the Churches will know that I am he who searches hearts and reins, and I will give to each of you according to your works (Apoc. 2). These things, brothers, are greatly to be guarded against, and the precepts of the Lord and the admonitions of the holy apostolic see, which discharges its commission in the place of the Lord the Saviour, are to be faithfully embraced and carried out. For the rest, brothers, concerning the question of the province, on which you formerly wished to consult the apostolic see [Hincmar 55, c. 13], it seems to us to have been sufficiently treated by our holy predecessors. But since you have thought fit to ask our lowliness again about the same matter, know that a province properly so called is one that has ten or eleven cities and one king, and as many lesser authorities under him, and one bishop, and ten or eleven other suffragan bishops as judges, to whose judgement all cases of bishops and of the other priests, and the cases of cities, are to be referred, so that they may be decided justly by all of these with a concordant voice, unless an appeal has been made to a higher authority by those who are to be judged. Hence no province ought to be degraded or dishonoured, but it should have within itself judges, priests and bishops, each, that is, according to their ranks. And whoever has a case, let him be judged by his own judges (a), and not by others, that is, by the just judges of his own province and not by outsiders, unless (as already stated) an appeal has been made by those judged. But if questions arise in any province, and the bishops of that province begin to differ in their reasoning, and they do not come to agreement among themselves in their disagreement, then let them be referred to the greater see. And if these are not decided easily and justly, let them be judged canonically and justly where a synod has been regularly assembled. But the greater and difficult questions [Innocent, letter 2] (as the holy synod has decreed and blessed custom requires) are always to be referred to the apostolic see. Furthermore, following the statutes of the holy Fathers, by synodal authority we decree that all who arm themselves against the Fathers (b), as assailants and slayers of the Fathers, are infamous: since those wounds which are not healed by poultices must be cut away or cured with the knife (c). Therefore, brothers, let unjust rivalries cease, let plots cease, let false accusations cease, lest any weak one, for whom Christ died, be torn by such plots; lest a sheep redeemed at the price of Christ be wounded by a brother's wolfish bites. Rightly then does the blame fall on us [St Celestine, letter 1] if we begin to favour such men. Let such things always be checked, and let those who attempt to practise them, or who plot against fathers or brothers, not be granted freedom to speak, nor be permitted to utter speech at their will. It is altogether clear that those who permit them to say such things connive with them; for truth would come forward if falsehood and calumny, or hatred, were displeasing. Let falsehood therefore cease to assail truth; let suspicion, which is justly repelled, cease to lie in wait; let hatred and enmity cease to persecute fathers or brothers; let conspiracy, which is to be repudiated by all, cease to harass teachers. Therefore the authors or perpetrators of these vices are not to be admitted in an accusation of bishops, but utterly rejected: since the canonical decrees of the Fathers command that the accusation or testimony of those who pursue anyone with hatred, or who are held to be enemies or suspect, be in no way admitted. Confirming their statutes, we too decree that all are to hold them inviolably in all future times. And whatever our fathers thought worthy to be decreed on this matter, it is necessary, as is fitting, that when it begins to be weakened or undermined, it be confirmed and renewed again by apostolic authority and given to the brothers. Given on the Kalends of March, in the year (d) of the Lord 587, in the fifth indiction.
