LETTER VII.
COPY OF THE LETTER OF PELAGIUS, POPE OF THE CITY OF ROME, TO AUNARIUS, BISHOP OF AUXERRE.
Pelagius to his most beloved brother Aunarius.

The more you render yourselves pleasing to God by veneration of the apostolic see, the more favourable the confidence of your charity becomes to him whose see it is. Nor do we confess the one and only Church of God in any other way than that we all be built upon the rock on which the catholic faith is founded. For this reason the desires of your Love have met with fulfilment, and with ready speed, since the relics sought are those of the princes from whom the preaching of the truth took its beginning. That you report that new churches abound in your regions we receive with rejoicing; yet if you knowingly embrace the zeal to pursue the prophetic word, "seek his face always." For the more the truth of the incarnation of our Lord is opened to human understanding, the more it is both honoured and worshipped. And just as you desire to be commended to God by our prayers, so you too bring the constant comfort of intercession to our needs and distresses, with which we are unceasingly burdened, praying and working to that end with whatever strength you can, so that, as you are in accord with the preaching of the apostolic see, so your prayer may rejoice together in its peace and quiet. May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the day before the Kalends of November, in the reign of the lord Maurice Tiberius, emperor Augustus, in the fifth year, in the fifth indiction.
DECREES OF PELAGIUS.
WHICH ARE ATTRIBUTED TO THE SECOND [PELAGIUS] FROM GRATIAN. VIII.
Pope Pelagius to Antonina, patrician lady, and Decia.

Concerning the bearer of this letter, let it cause you no distress of mind that he has not been made a defensor, for truly I find it most bitter that men should be led from that way of life to that office in which the things promised to God by monks can in no way be fulfilled. For the difference between that habit and this office is complete. There, there is quiet, prayer, the labour of the hands; but here, the hearing of cases, summonses, proceedings, public lawsuits, and whatever either the institutions of the Church or the need of petitioners may require. May God grant that those who are either brought up by us in that habit or grow up in monasteries be such that, when advanced in age and proven in life, they may be promoted not to the offices of litigation but to the priesthood.
IX.
Pope Pelagius to bishop Florentinus. Whoever after death, etc.

Having received the report of your Fraternity, we have learned that its bearer has indeed not entered a second marriage; yet you indicated that he did not keep chastity in his former marriage. And although there are many things which the authority of [canonical] strictness commands to be canonically observed in cases of this kind, nevertheless, because the failing of our times, in which not only men's merits but their very bodies have failed, does not allow the rigour of that severity to remain in all things, and the age of this man in question is recognised to remove suspicion of future incontinence, know that, condescending, as has been said, to the failing of the times, we have granted that he may be advanced to the diaconate. And further on: As for his maidservant Miscena, by whom he has confessed he had children after his wife's death, we order that by your arrangement she be handed over to some monastery of continent women, to make profession there.
X.
Pope Pelagius to the clergy of Catania. He who is elected bishop, etc.

We sent some time ago such a letter to our brother and fellow bishop Eucarpus concerning the visitation of the church of Catania that you could have learned our judgement from it. However, since we have learned, also from your report, that certain persons there are stirring up dissensions, not with sound intention but from wicked aims, who, knowing that they cannot be brought to the episcopate by age, learning or merits of life, wish to disturb the Church only so that the future bishop may promise them impunity for what they have presumptuously taken from it, and the ambition for the episcopate may become a security for plunder, we have thought it right to admonish you also of this: that you hasten, God willing, to bring to us the decree made for the deacon Elpidius and signed by all whom your report named, together with the letter of the aforesaid visitor and with that same deacon. And after a little: So when our son the magnificent Leo, the praetor, came here, he told us of the individual matters that have been stirred up there, and how the wishes of almost the whole city agreed on the deacon Elpidius. Therefore, since we can in no way doubt the testimony of the said man, for this reason, as has been said, make the deacon Elpidius hasten to us, and do not wait any longer for our admonition to have to be sent to him. Him, however, we specially admonish through your Love in this present command that he promise no one that he gives or will give anything; nor dare to grant or promise anyone any security concerning past church matters; nor, as if made bishop, fail to reclaim what has been plundered, but rather freely allow it to remain with those by whom it was plundered: knowing that if he has done or shall do any such thing, not only is that promise in no way permitted by us to stand, but also, with the loss of the judgement we had formed of him, he will not be able to earn the rank of pastoral consecration.
XI.
Pope Pelagius to Cresconius, an illustrious man. On the exactions of bishops.

We wish you to ensure by all means that none of the bishops of Sicily presume to take more than two solidi from the parishes belonging to them under the name of the cathedraticum, nor compel the priests or clergy of their parishes to prepare banquets for them beyond their means.
XII.
Pope Pelagius to Benegestus the defensor. Clerics are not to be accused before a civil judge.

By the present authority we command your Experience that in cases in which any person of ecclesiastical office stands in the place of plaintiff, intending to sue some layman, he should not fail to bring his actions before the judge of his province. But in those matters in which a person of ecclesiastical office is sued, every obstacle to the suit being removed, he is without distinction to appear for examination before the bishop or the priests established in the place where the dispute arises.
XIII.
Likewise to Sergius the chancellor.

If any cleric, whether of lower or higher rank, is the plaintiff and directs his actions against a lay person, he is by all means to appear to plead his case nowhere but before the judge of the province. But if any layman thinks a cleric of any rank should be sued, let him bring the actions which he thinks he has before the judgement of the bishops established in the same city or territory. That this order is shown to be in every respect agreeable and consistent with the laws is made plain by that rule which prescribes that the plaintiff always follow the court of the defendant. And that for clerics who are sued the proper court lies in the episcopal judgement, the authority of imperial sanctions also declares.
FRAGMENTS OF THE LETTERS OF PELAGIUS II.

The authority to convene synods has been committed to the apostolic see by special power, nor do we read that any general synod is valid which was not convened or supported by its authority. This canonical authority attests, this ecclesiastical history corroborates, this the holy Fathers confirm.
XIV.
Pelagius to Eucarpus, bishop of Messina.

We believe, according to the Apostle, that the charity with which we have always loved your Love surpasses all things, and that no labour for the state of the Church is burdensome to your Holiness. Your Fraternity knows that, for our sins, all seek their own things, not those of Jesus Christ. We have said this beforehand because we again enjoin on you the visitation of the church of Catania, whose bishop, as we have learned from the report of the clergy we received, has passed from this light. (For it is impossible for us, in that province, at least in the parts about Syracuse, to entrust to anyone else the matters that pertain to God, unless perhaps God should now wish such a one to be chosen through you at Catania, of whose conscience we can be secure, so that we may relieve you of these labours a little.) So let your Love go at once to the aforesaid church of Catania, and with God's help urge and persuade that a man from the clergy be elected who has neither a wife, nor children, nor any crime hostile to the canons, and send him at once to the city of Rome with the decree and the attestation of your report.
THE SAME.

Having received the report of your Fraternity, we have learned that its bearer has indeed not entered a second marriage; yet you indicated that he did not keep chastity in his former marriage. And although there are many things which the authority of strictness commands to be observed in cases of this kind, nevertheless, because the failing of our times, in which not only men's merits but their very bodies have failed, does not allow the rigour of that severity to remain in all things, and the age of this man in question is recognised to remove suspicion of future incontinence, know that, condescending, as has been said, to the failing of the times, we have granted that he may be advanced to the order of the diaconate; on this condition, however, that you render account to our common Lord on the Day of Judgement before that terrible tribunal for his morals and life and conduct: for we so soften past things on account of the straits of the time as to meet future excesses cautiously and carefully. For this reason we order that Micina the maidservant, by whom he has confessed he had children after his wife's death, may not remain with him, and that by your arrangement she be handed over to some monastery to profess continence, so that, by a better lot, he may serve in the office to which he is promoted with the merit of good repute, and no occasion be left for staining his reputation (Gratian, Dist. 34, chapter Fraternitatis).
DECREES OF PELAGIUS II,
From Gratian and others.
THE COLLECTOR'S NOTICE.

Labbe gave certain decrees of Pope Pelagius II from Gratian, but collected in such a way that he left out some. So that nothing may be lacking to a full collection of these decrees, I have taken up here, to be supplied, those that escaped his diligence.
XV.
Pope Pelagius to the clergy of Narni.

Our brother and fellow bishop John, prompted by zeal for the Church's benefit, and having weighed the simplicity of his own nature with praiseworthy reflection, admits that he is hardly fit to bear the care of governing the patrimony or to maintain church discipline. He therefore asks that the person of the priest Constitutus be assigned to him to carry these things out, so that what is necessary may be done under fitting care in its arrangement, and nothing unseemly or useless be allowed to be done. Therefore by the present command we instruct you that, keeping first of all the reverence toward the said bishop which it befits you to show blamelessly, you give fitting obedience to Constitutus in all things that pertain to the service of divine worship, or that care for the Church's benefit may advise to be done, in nothing resisting his arrangements with a stubborn spirit, but rather, with the fitting zeal of your vigilance, fulfilling whatever Constitutus advises to be done for the Church's benefit; so that, with these things so arranged, your customary stipends may be supplied to you, and whatever is necessary in the patrimony of the said church, or in recovering things belonging to it, may be accomplished.
XVI.
Pope Pelagius II to Oplio, defensor.

We leave to the monks henceforth no power and no licence, at their own will, either to expel the abbot or to ordain others for themselves, since no authority will remain to the abbot if he begins to be subject to the power of the monks; so that henceforth the care of the abbot, to whom all power ought to belong, must faithfully and zealously fulfil all things that pertain to reverence for divine worship or to the benefit of the same monastery. (Gratian, XVIII, q. 2, chapter Nullam.)
APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS AND DECREES OF POPE PELAGIUS II.
LETTER [formerly I].
TO ARCHBISHOP BENIGNUS.
He condemns the transfer of bishops from one church to another when the Church's benefit does not require it.
To his most beloved brother Archbishop Benignus, Bishop Pelagius.

Having read the letter of your Fraternity (St Leo, letter 3), we have recognised the vigour of your faith, which we had long known, congratulating your Love that you vigilantly devote pastoral care to guarding the flock of Christ and are solicitous for those subject to you. For good deeds also make for our joy (St Celestine, letter 2); and if anything turns out otherwise than it should, it troubles us with no small grief. For divine grace grants great rejoicing (Council of Toledo X) when it allows us to exchange by letter the rule of saving discipline, and brings about what we long for in the pursuits of peacemakers. Your Love therefore seeks the counsel of the apostolic see (Zosimus) as to whether it is lawful for a bishop to pass over, or to change, from city to city, since certain canons (as it seems to you) forbid this to be done. You have also indicated in your letter that for reasons of benefit you wish to transfer a certain brother, a servant of God in name and deed, to the place and city of one deceased, although some say that this may not be done, even if you had the consent of the apostolic see. Know therefore, most beloved brother, that a cause of necessity and benefit is one thing, and a cause of presumption and self-will another. So he does not change his see who does not change his mind, that is, who moves from city to city not for avarice, or domination, or self-will, or his own choice, but is changed for necessity or benefit. For the benefit of many is to be preferred to the benefit or will of one. For to change is one thing, and to be changed another; just as to minister is one thing, and to be ministered to another. Hence the Lord speaks in the Gospel, saying: I came not to be ministered to, but to minister (Matt. 20). For what is read in the canons, that a bishop ought not to pass (Council of Antioch, canon 21), or be transferred, from city to city, is not said of those who do this either expelled by force, or compelled by necessity, or by the authority of their superiors, but of those who, inflamed with the heat of avarice, leap forward of their own accord, and desire to serve ambition rather than the benefit of the Church, and press on so as to exercise domination. Hence it is also contained in the canons below: If anyone should prove rash (Council of Sardica, canon 2), who perhaps offers the excuse that he received letters from the people and therefore moved, while it is clear that a few, who do not have sincere faith, could have been corrupted by reward and payment to shout in the church and seem to ask for him, we decree that such frauds must be entirely removed. From these words and many other examples it is clear that it does not speak (as was touched on a little above) of those who pass from city to city driven out, or not received by the citizens or by anyone else, or under the pressure of necessity, or by the authority of superiors; but of those who leap forward of their own accord, and do this out of rashness or ambition. For to pass over of one's own accord is one thing, and to come under compulsion or necessity another. Hence these do not change cities, but are changed: for they do this not of their own accord but under compulsion. For who ever dares to say that St Peter, prince of the apostles, did not act well when he changed his see from Antioch to Rome? Or who denies that he is a saint on that account, or that he ever lost the merit of the apostolate, in heaven or on earth? Or who denies that many other bishops are saints who were transferred from cities to cities, or says they lost the merit of the episcopate; whose names, if I began to list them, the day would pass before I could write all these out, and the letter would be longer than necessary? Or who can ever establish that Alexander was not a saint, who was transferred to Jerusalem from another city (Socrates VII, c. 36)? or St Gregory Nazianzen, who was appointed in Nazianzus? or St Proclus, who was transferred from Cyzicus and enthroned at Constantinople? So those do not rightly understand the church rules who deny that this can be done for reasons of benefit or necessity, whenever common benefit or necessity urges it. For we find none of these, or of others who by better counsel changed cities through some necessity or ecclesiastical benefit, deprived of lay communion, nor should this ever by any means be done. As for the decision found in the council of Antioch (canon 21), that a bishop should by no means move from one diocese to another, it as a whole, and all decisions on that matter, keep the force set out above, and in no way harm, in the manner already stated, translations of bishops done or to be done, but rather lend them strength and the authority of [the word of] the Lord Saviour, which is exalted above all canonical books. Such questions, however, seem to arise more from envy than from charity or benefit, since Truth itself says: If they persecute you in one city, flee to another (Matt. 10), and the rest. No catholic can anywhere contradict this decision, which is known to have been uttered and confirmed not by another but by the Lord's own mouth. If anyone contradicts it, let him be driven from the Church not only as an exile but also anathematised. And the Lord says elsewhere in the Gospel: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake (Matt. 5). If the Lord calls those blessed who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, who can condemn them? And if he himself commands flight from city to city because of persecution, who dares or is able to disparage or condemn them because they obey the Lord's words? Surely he who contradicts or resists condemns himself, since he proves stubborn and disobedient to the mouth of the Lord. Hence Truth itself says: Which of you convicts me of sin? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? He who is of God hears the words of God. You do not hear them because you are not of God (John 8). We must by all means obey God rather than men (Acts 5). And because we obey God, and pass from city to city (at his command) on account of persecution, that is, of necessity or benefit, are we to be condemned? Not at all, but rather to be revered and supported, since this cannot be imputed to the bishops themselves either. He who resists these surely resists the ordinance of God, and is worse than an unbeliever: for it is better not to know the way of truth than to turn back after knowing it. For the Lord himself withdrew from place to place, that is, passed over, when the Jews were seeking him. Fleeing those who sought and persecuted him, he gave us an example to flee those who persecute, and to pass from city to city, saying: If they persecute you in this city, flee to another (Matt. 10), and other things like these. For if to flee is bad (Tripartite History, VI, c. 22, from St Athanasius' apology for his flight), to persecute is much worse. The one hides so as not to die; the other persecutes so as to kill; and flight is commanded, because he who seeks to kill transgresses the law and rather gives occasion for flight. If the persecutors reproach flight, let them rather be ashamed of themselves and cease to lay snares, and those fleeing will at once cease. For no one ever flees a gentle man, but rather one who is fierce and cunning together. For everyone who was groaning and harassed by Saul fled and came to David (1 Kgs 22). If, then, the most pious and most just David had known it to be a sin for people fleeing persecution to pass from place to place and from city to city, he would by no means have received such men, nor kept them with him, nor settled them in other cities. For those who persecute the Lord's bishops and compel them to pass from city to city persecute not so much them as our Lord Jesus Christ, whose embassy they carry out. Nor do the bishops themselves sin in this, since they do it not willingly but under compulsion; rather those by whom they are persecuted [sin]. Nor can this be imputed to the bishops themselves, but to those who compel them to do it. For the holy protomartyr Stephen was being stoned, but Jesus was receiving the blows. And therefore each person must take care (Hadrian, collection, ch. 66) not to persecute, judge or punish anyone unjustly, lest he persecute, judge and punish Jesus. And those who deny that mercy should be shown to those who flee and to those who suffer necessity deny Christ himself, who is mercy and truth, and who commands that help be given to all who suffer necessity. The things I have asserted are few, brother; but how much hangs on them your foresight will be able to judge. Why do the malevolent strive to break in upon this mercy (Ennodius, in his apology for Pope Symmachus)? Why mock happiness with empty contentions? This madness no longer has any excuse among believers; nor does it matter by what roads he runs to the prince of this world who departs from the goodwill of the brethren or denies mercy to those who suffer necessity. He denies mercy to those who suffer necessity who does not permit, for people in need of the divine mysteries and having no bishop of their own to instruct them, a more learned or more useful bishop to be moved, for reasons of benefit and necessity, from another city (even if it is smaller) to the one that has no bishop, by better counsel, passing not of his own will but at the exhortation of his superiors; or who does not permit a bishop who has been expelled and is suffering persecution to be enthroned for reasons of benefit or necessity. For among the ancients (Tripartite History, XII, ch. 8, from Socrates), a bishop used to move from one city to another without any distinction, whenever benefit or necessity called him. For this reason it has seemed good to insert the rule itself in this letter as well, to show that those who said that a bishop cannot be enthroned have lied. Hence it reads thus in the canons (VII, ch. 6; Council of Antioch, canon 18): If any bishop who has been ordained does not go to the diocese for which he was ordained, not through his own fault but either because the people reject him or for some other cause arising from necessity, we decree that he is to share in the honour and the ministry, yet not to interfere in the affairs of the church in which he celebrates the assemblies, but also to accept whatever the synod of the province has determined by its judgement. No one can contradict this rule, which also orders a bishop to be enthroned for reasons of benefit or necessity, and allows him to be moved and to pass from one city to another city that has no bishop of its own. He offers fat victims to the devil (Ennodius, already cited) who strives to resist these things, or denies mercy and benefit to the Church, to those already mentioned, that is, both to bishops and to peoples. In vain, then, will they henceforth lay snares against the simple, who once, saying these things, forbade them to be done, since, armed with these and other supports, they will know what is to be done in these matters and what is to be avoided. For he is very well armed (the same Ennodius, ibid.) who scorns the weapons that the adversary of mercy, benefit and concord supplies. Against all the darts of quarrels, then, the bare opposition of faith suffices. I know you are not unaware, brother, that the cited sentences of the canons and the sanctions of the Gospel are not new, but are made subject to our assent. Why do those who contradict them, and who forbid the migrations of bishops made for reasons of benefit and necessity, and not, as has often been said, of avarice or rashness, to the ruin of priests and peoples, injure priestly counsel? Why do they tear apart a judgement in which, by Christ's inspiration, heavenly oracles were revealed, and the tongue of the pontiffs stood as interpreter between God and men? For that court of heaven, enriched with the endowments of various curule seats and adorned with much gold and purple of our Redeemer, put forward nothing in that decision on its own authority, but through the ministry of a human tongue served the divine command. It understood that whatever it established under impulse was not its own; and it has nothing in that judgement except that over which it may rejoice for its devotion alone. For while the profane words of the persons mentioned are believed, they betray both the ignorance of their madness and their envy. What room is there here for error, where the words of example and of history run together in agreement along an equal course? Nor is what is put forward different from catholic understanding and the readings. For it is not well to look for a knot in a bulrush, while a fog wraps the authors of the light that is preached. Foul, too, and released from the obligation of his Lord's splendour is he who pays his duties to the heavenly statutes with less than pure faith. The sayings or prohibitions of such men, then, become unworthy even of mention. Very deep, then, is their ignorance, and their throat is an open sepulchre, for with their tongues they act deceitfully (Ps. 5, in St Jerome's version). For there is nothing right in their mouth, their inward parts are snares, their heart is choked with dense briars (these are the words of the same Ennodius), and they strive to ascribe their inner vices to others. He therefore gives nobility to crimes who takes their airing of such matters as an example, or passes it on to the ears of posterity with a worthy account. But do not concern yourself with such questions; follow the judgement of the blessed apostle Paul, who warns everyone through his disciple and cries out, saying: Avoid empty questions (1 Tim. 4). Always avoid empty questions, then (according to the Apostle), and do what you have usefully perceived ought to be done by better counsel, not for reasons of avarice or rashness, but of benefit and necessity (as has often been said). Therefore, dearest one, supported by these apostolic authorities, move the bishop about whom you wished to consult us, for reasons of necessity or benefit; and teach our other brothers, whom necessity or benefit has compelled to do this, to act [likewise]: for what we write to you alone, we command all in general to hold. For just as we have the power to assign bishops and priests to titles and to ordain them according to the rule, so (as has been said above) for reasons of necessity or benefit you have [the power] both to move [them] and to transfer [them] from title to title, even if one must be moved from a lesser to a greater city. This, however, must above all be guarded against, that it never be done out of arrogance or avarice: for it is these who are condemned by the aforesaid canons, not those who do this out of necessity or benefit, by the counsel of their superiors, and with a sound, pure intention pleasing to God. You, brother, always pursue justice, piety, faith, charity, patience and gentleness (1 Tim. 6). Fight also the good fight of faith, and lay hold of eternal life, to which you have been called: for the spirit of those who fear the Lord is sought by him, and in his regard is blessed. For their hope is in him who saves them, and the eyes of God are on those who love him. He who fears the Lord will tremble at nothing and will not be afraid, for he himself is his hope. Blessed is the soul of him who fears the Lord: to whom does he look, and who is his strength? The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him: a protector of might, a support of strength, a shelter from the heat and a shade at noon, a safeguard against stumbling and a help in falling, raising up the soul and enlightening the eyes, giving health and life and blessing. The offering of one who sacrifices from wrongdoing is stained, and the mockeries of the unjust are not well pleasing; the Lord [is] for those alone who wait for him in the way of truth and justice. The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked, nor does he look upon the offerings of the unjust, nor will he be propitiated for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices. He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who slaughters a son in the sight of his father. The bread of the needy is the life of the poor: he who defrauds him of it is a man of blood; he who takes away bread earned in sweat, and food from the one who sweats, is like one who kills his neighbour. He who sheds blood and he who defrauds a hired labourer are brothers. One building and one tearing down: what do they gain but toil? One praying, one cursing: whose voice will God hear? He who is washed after touching a dead body and touches it again, what does his washing profit? So a man who fasts for his sins and does the same things again, what does he profit by humbling himself? Who will hear his prayer? He who keeps the law multiplies prayer. It is a saving sacrifice to heed the commandments and to depart from all wickedness; and it is propitiation, offering sacrifice for injustices; and entreaty for sins, to withdraw from injustice. He who offers fine flour repays a favour; and he who does mercy offers sacrifice. It is well pleasing to the Lord to withdraw from wickedness; and [it is] entreaty to withdraw from injustice. You shall not appear empty before the sight of God. For all these things are done because of the commandment of the Lord. The offering of the just enriches the altar, and is a sweet fragrance in the sight of the Most High. The sacrifice of the just is acceptable, and the Lord will not forget his memorial. Give glory to God with a good spirit, and do not diminish the firstfruits of your crops. In every gift make your face cheerful, and sanctify your tithes with exultation. Give to the Most High according to what he has given, and with a good eye make [an offering of] what your hands have found, for the Lord is one who repays, and will give back to you sevenfold. Do not offer crooked gifts; for he will not accept them. And do not look to an unjust sacrifice, for the Lord is judge, and with him there is no regard for persons. The Lord will not show partiality against the poor, and he will hear the prayer of the wronged. He will not despise the prayers of the orphan, nor the widow, if she pours out her speech of lament. Do not the widow's tears run down her cheek, and her outcry [rise] against the one who causes them? For from the cheek they go up as far as heaven, and the Lord who hears will not take delight in them. He who worships God will be received with delight, and his prayer will draw near even to the clouds. The prayer of one who humbles himself will pierce the clouds; and until it draws near he will not be comforted. And he will not depart until the Most High looks on: and the Lord will not delay, but will judge the unjust and execute judgement, and the Mighty One will have no patience with them, so that he may crush their backs and render vengeance to the nations, until he removes the fullness of the proud and crushes the sceptres of the wicked, until he renders to all according to their deeds, and according to the works of Adam and according to his presumption, until he judges the cause of his people and delights the just with his mercy. And may God (dearest brother) fulfil your desire and the ministry divinely conferred on you, according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus our Lord. And to God our Father be glory for ever and ever. Amen. Given on the 13th day of the month of August, in the 14th indiction.
LETTER [formerly II]
TO THE BISHOPS OF ITALY
That bishops are to be held in the highest honour, and cannot be accused by just anyone.
To his most beloved and most illustrious brothers, all the bishops, and especially all those serving the Lord throughout the provinces of Campania and Italy, Pelagius [sends] greeting.

Bearing about the care of all the Churches (as the Apostle says), we ought to be mindful of the divine grace towards us (Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, letter to Pope Simplicius): the Lord, through the mercy of his condescension, has raised us to this priestly eminence so that, holding fast to his commands and set as it were on a watchtower of his priests, we may forbid what is unlawful and teach what is to be followed (Pope Hilary, letter to Ascanius, bishop of Tarragona). All, dearest ones, who wish to live piously in Christ (2 Tim. 3) must suffer reproaches from the impious and from those unlike them (Prosper, Sentence 32, from St Augustine on Psalm 122), and be despised as fools and madmen who lose present goods for this reason, that they may acquire invisible goods that will profit them. But this contempt and mockery will be turned back on [the mockers] themselves, when their abundance has passed into want and their pride into confusion. For by a just judgement power is often given to sinners (the same, Sentence 23, from St Augustine on Psalm 118) by which to persecute his saints, so that those who are helped and led by the Spirit of God may become more glorious through the exercise of their labours. And although, brothers, these things are so, those who rebuke or accuse their prelates are nonetheless not to be agreed with, but rejected. Therefore, following and strengthening the canonical statutes of the holy Fathers, so that the pillars of holy Church may not totter, we wholly remove from every accusation of bishops all who are infamous, all who are suspect or hostile, and those who are not of their nation, or whose faith, life and free status are unknown, and who are not of good conduct, or whose life is open to accusation. Likewise we judge that all those whom the divine laws call dead are to be removed from the same accusation and submitted to public penance. Nor, while the churches, possessions or property of any bishop are being held, not of his own will, by his rivals or by any others whatever, ought or can anything be charged against him by anyone before the restoration of all his property; but first everything must be restored to him according to the laws, and afterwards, at the time fixed by the Fathers, the matters are to be examined. Robbers, thieves, the sacrilegious, adulterers and the like are also to be rejected. For it is clear that such people always pursue discord rather than peace. Nor may any monk ever take up such things, or presume to disturb secular or ecclesiastical affairs, for in such matters their voice is dead. For the Lord wishes his chief preachers always to remain unshaken, and not to be violated by certain people, but to serve him freely and quietly. Hence he himself says: Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye. And whoever grieves you grieves me (Zech. 2; Col. 3). And: whoever does wrong will receive [back] the wrong he has done (Matt. 10). And elsewhere: Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever scorns you scorns me (Luke 10). So too the shepherds and preachers of the Church are to be feared, borne with and revered by the peoples and by all others generally, so that under the exercise of good will temporal things may be endured (Prosper, Sentence 34, from Augustine on Psalm 124) [and] eternal things hoped for. For he increases the merits of virtue who does not violate, but increases, his religious purpose. Charity indeed always renews a man (the same, Sentence 273). And as malice makes men old, so love makes them new. The faith of those who are to see God (the same, Sentence 361) believes what it does not see. For if it sees, it is not faith. Merit is gathered for the one who believes; the reward is rendered to the one who sees. The shepherd's diadem is precious (Ennodius, in the address beginning 'episc.') when the Church's flock does not resist his persuasion as it advances towards uprightness. He loves his admonisher without pretence and with truthful mouth who follows his instructions. The institutions of nature and admonitions offer men an answer. The return of clamorous anxiety comes back to mortals, because each will receive according to what he has done. For the favour that tongues have received perishes in vain (the same, Letter 22, book 7), unless the business has been lawfully begun and canonically completed. For what apostolic authority commands is sent out in confidence in our side. You only, prelates of Christ, always show your kindness, preserving fairness of ears and minds (the same, address 21), and good will. For to help against assaults, and to bring back the wanderer after an interval, is justice. For he offers prosperity to the Lord who drives adversity away from the afflicted (Council of Toledo VIII, c. 1). The fruit, venerable prelates, is appointed for labours, to be rendered with judgement most purely, so that in both cases a fitting lustre may neither disfigure the receiver, if it comes from an unworthy source (from the same Ennodius, address 21), nor, if it is conferred undeservedly, stain the giver. Let there always be a free voice against the depraved and impious and the persecutors of the servants of God, and let them be struck and refuted with the sword of the mouth. Let them be pursued and driven back, confounded and turned away, and let them have no opportunity of harming those who live piously. Very often what seems safest is full of dangers (from the same, in the Life of the monk Antony). See with what great snares such men toil: therefore what we hear may not be hidden. Our persecution was already hidden, [now it is] manifest: strictness maintained towards persecutors and criminals is mercy. Therefore grant quiet to rest: drive away also the enemy of the heavenly commandments, lest the bright conduct of those living with you be violated by the dark contagion of one who comes in. For remedies must be provided before the disease grows. Let us also seek the army of the holy apostles and of the other priests, and shut the mouths of the aforesaid persecutors. The conduct of the world is restrained by fear of the laws (the same, Letter 13, book 5): ecclesiastical custody too is preserved and governed by the reins of the rules. May God, dearest one, always turn envy far away (the same, Letter 14 of the same book). Arm yourselves therefore (as the Apostle says) with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, and with the shield of apostolic authority (Eph. 6), so that the rights of the Church's fruitfulness may not be overthrown by any blow of a raging storm (the same, ibid.). Never burden anyone with any prejudgement, but always look to what is declared by the testimony of the rules. It remains, holy prelates, that you always hasten devoutly to the joys of the brothers, for divine benefits always come by degrees, and to those on whom they confer good things they promise better. For one always ascends by increments to the summit where heavenly favour provides the beginning. May almighty God always guard what he has granted, and increase with successes what will be profitable (the same, Letter 19, book 5). For let all your things, brothers, always be done in charity (1 Cor. 16). And do not disparage those who disparage, since to disparage those who disparage is not good, lest, stirred against what is written, we should make a contest (Deusdedit of Cagliari, consultation 4 of the Lateran Council, in the year 649). We must not at all fear the reproach of men, nor be overcome by their taunts (Pope Martin I, consultation 1 of the same council), since the Lord commands us this through the prophet Isaiah, saying: Hear me, you who know judgement, my people, in whose hearts is my law. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not fear their blasphemies (Isa. 51), considering what is written in the psalm: Will not God search these things out? For he knows the secrets of the heart, and the thoughts of such men, that they are vain. Each has spoken vain things to his neighbour: deceitful lips, with a double heart they have spoken evil. But may the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue. Who have said: We will magnify our tongue, our lips are our own, who is our Lord? (Ps. 43; Ps. 93; Ps. 11). For if they kept these things in memory, they would by no means leap forth into such great iniquity. For they do not do this through approved and fatherly teaching, but in order to exercise their own vengeance on the servants of God (the same, Martin, ibid.). For it is written: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes (Prov. 12). And: There are ways which seem just to a man, but their ends lead to death (Prov. 14). For we who suffer these things ought to reserve them to the judgement of God, who will render to each according to his works (Matt. 16). He also thundered through his ministers, saying: Vengeance is mine, I will repay (Rom. 12). Do you, then, in right and pure faith and in good will, help one another in turn, and let no one withdraw his hand from supporting his brother: for by this (says the Lord) all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another (John 13). Given on the Kalends of December, in the 15th indiction (in the year of the Lord 581).
LETTER [formerly IX]
TO THE BISHOPS OF GERMANY AND GAUL
That nine prefaces, to be sung during the solemnities of the Mass,
are received by the Roman Church.
Pelagius, bishop of the Roman church and of the apostolic see, to all the bishops of the regions of the Germanies and the Gauls (St Leo, letter 88).

When, in the name of God, we had held a synod of bishops and of the other faithful fellow priests of God assembled in the Roman Church, and were treating more carefully of the ecclesiastical statutes, as they have been handed down by the apostles and the holy Fathers, your letter arrived, and, so that it might carry great authority, living voices also went before it, asking that we send back to you in our letter the order of prefaces which the holy Roman Church has held until now. Then we rejoiced greatly at your desire and so good a zeal, and, carefully rereading the sacred Roman order and the sacred constitutions of our predecessors, we found that only these nine prefaces are to be received in the sacred catalogue, which long-standing truth has preserved in the Roman Church until now: one in the Easter Albs, another for the Ascension of the Lord, the third for Pentecost, the fourth for the Nativity of the Lord, the fifth for the Appearing of the Lord, the sixth for the apostles, the seventh for the Holy Trinity, the eighth for the Cross, the ninth to be said only in the fast and in Lent. These prefaces the holy Roman Church holds and keeps. We command you to hold them.
